chapters.title: About SP 800-53
chapters.summary: What the catalog is, who uses it, its history, and the documents around it.

blocks.text: **NIST Special Publication 800-53 Revision 5**, *Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations*, is a catalog of security and privacy controls. It tells you **what safeguards exist** and what each one requires. It does not tell you which ones to pick: that is the job of the baselines in **SP 800-53B** and of your risk assessment.

items: **Mandatory** for US federal information systems under FISMA and OMB Circular A-130, and the basis of FedRAMP for cloud services sold to US agencies.
**Voluntary** everywhere else, but widely used by banks, critical infrastructure operators, cloud providers and consultancies worldwide as the most detailed public control catalog.
**Public domain** and free, which is why so many other frameworks map to it.

blocks.title: Why a non-US organisation should care
blocks.text: Many frameworks you already use (CSF 2.0, ISO 27001 mappings, cloud provider compliance reports, FedRAMP, CMMC) point back to SP 800-53. Knowing it lets you read any control mapping and understand what "good" looks like at a detailed level.

blocks.text: What changed in Rev. 5

items: **Outcome-based controls:** "The organization..." and "The information system..." removed, so controls apply to any entity (organisation, system, provider).
**Privacy integrated** into the main catalog rather than an appendix, with a new **PT** family.
**Supply chain** raised to a full **SR** family.
**Baselines separated** into SP 800-53B, so the catalog can serve non-federal users.
**New controls** for areas such as cyber resiliency, threat hunting (RA-10), and secure engineering.

blocks.text: Organisation-defined parameters

ODPs make controls flexible. For example, AC-7 requires enforcing a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts during [Assignment: organization-defined time period]. You fill in the values (e.g. 5 attempts in 15 minutes) in your system security plan. Baselines, overlays or regulators may set them for you.
A value you define, such as a number, time period, personnel or roles.
A choice from listed options, e.g. [Selection (one or more): lock the account; delay next logon prompt; notify administrator].

blocks.title: ODPs are where assessments fail
blocks.text: A control statement with blank ODPs is not implementable or testable. Assessors check that every ODP has a value, that the value is justified, and that the system actually enforces it.

sections.title: How to read the control pages in this book

items: **Card label:** control ID, then the SP 800-53B baselines it belongs to. **L** = Low, **M** = Moderate, **H** = High, **P** = Privacy, **None** = not in any baseline (selected only through tailoring or overlays).
**Card text:** the control title and a plain-English summary (written for this book).
**In practice:** an excerpt from NIST's own discussion for the control.
**Example:** an illustrative scenario written for this book.
**Control statement:** NIST's requirement text, with parameters shown as [Assignment] and [Selection] placeholders.
**Enhancements table:** every active enhancement with its baselines.
**Related controls:** NIST's cross-references.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A regional bank uses CSF 2.0 for board reporting and the SP 800-53 Moderate baseline as its internal control library. Each control has an owner and test procedure adapted from SP 800-53A, and results roll up to CSF subcategories.

The **Open Security Controls Assessment Language (OSCAL)** provides machine-readable formats (JSON, XML, YAML) for catalogs, baseline profiles, component definitions, system security plans, assessment plans and results, and POA&Ms. NIST publishes SP 800-53 and the 53B baselines in OSCAL, and FedRAMP accepts OSCAL-based packages.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.text: OSCAL lets GRC tools import the catalog, baselines and parameters exactly, and generate SSPs and assessment evidence without retyping. The control data in this book was taken from NIST's OSCAL catalog, Release 5.2.0.

blocks.text: Access Control governs who and what can access systems and information, and what they can do once in: accounts, enforcement of permissions, least privilege, remote and wireless access, and sessions.

blocks.title: Where most audits start
blocks.text: AC-2 (account management), AC-3 (access enforcement) and AC-6 (least privilege) are among the most frequently tested and most frequently failed controls. Get joiner-mover-leaver and privileged access right first.
Withdrawn controls

items: **AC-13** Supervision and Review — Access Control: incorporated into AC-2, AU-6
**AC-15** Automated Marking: incorporated into MP-3

blocks.text: **Policy and Procedures.** Write, approve and maintain an access control policy and procedures, name an official to manage them, and review them on a defined schedule.
blocks.practice: Access control policy and procedures address the controls in the AC family that are implemented within systems and organizations. The risk management strategy is an important factor in establishing such policies and procedures. Policies and procedures contribute to security and privacy assurance.
blocks.example: A bank's CISO owns the access control policy, reviewed annually and after a major audit finding on privileged access.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop, document, and disseminate to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined personnel or roles]:
**a.1.** [Selection (one or more): organization-level; mission/business process-level; system-level] access control policy that:
**a.1.(a).** Addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; and
**a.1.(b).** Is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; and
**a.2.** Procedures to facilitate the implementation of the access control policy and the associated access controls;
**b.** Designate an [Assignment: organization-defined official] to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the access control policy and procedures; and
**c.** Review and update the current access control:
**c.1.** Policy [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events] ; and
**c.2.** Procedures [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** IA-1, PM-9, PM-24, PS-8, SI-12.
**Account Management.** Manage the full lifecycle of system accounts: define account types, approve creation, assign managers, monitor use, and disable or remove accounts when no longer needed.
blocks.practice: Examples of system account types include individual, shared, group, system, guest, anonymous, emergency, developer, temporary, and service. Identification of authorized system users and the specification of access privileges reflect the requirements in other controls in the security plan.
blocks.example: HR termination events automatically disable Active Directory and SaaS accounts within an hour, and quarterly reviews remove stale accounts.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Define and document the types of accounts allowed and specifically prohibited for use within the system;
**b.** Assign account managers;
**c.** Require [Assignment: organization-defined prerequisites and criteria] for group and role membership;
**d.** Specify:
**d.1.** Authorized users of the system;
**d.2.** Group and role membership; and
**d.3.** Access authorizations (i.e., privileges) and [Assignment: organization-defined attributes (as required)] for each account;
**e.** Require approvals by [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] for requests to create accounts;
**f.** Create, enable, modify, disable, and remove accounts in accordance with [Assignment: organization-defined policy, procedures, prerequisites, and criteria];
**g.** Monitor the use of accounts;
**h.** Notify account managers and [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] within:
**h.1.** [Assignment: organization-defined time period] when accounts are no longer required;
**h.2.** [Assignment: organization-defined time period] when users are terminated or transferred; and
**h.3.** [Assignment: organization-defined time period] when system usage or need-to-know changes for an individual;
**i.** Authorize access to the system based on:
**i.1.** A valid access authorization;
**i.2.** Intended system usage; and
**i.3.** [Assignment: organization-defined attributes (as required)];
**j.** Review accounts for compliance with account management requirements [Assignment: organization-defined frequency];
**k.** Establish and implement a process for changing shared or group account authenticators (if deployed) when individuals are removed from the group; and
**l.** Align account management processes with personnel termination and transfer processes.

rows: **AC-2(2)** Automated Temporary and Emergency Account Management

**Access Enforcement.** Enforce approved authorisations so that users and processes can only access what they have been permitted to access.
blocks.practice: Access control policies control access between active entities or subjects (i.e., users or processes acting on behalf of users) and passive entities or objects (i.e., devices, files, records, domains) in organizational systems.
blocks.example: The claims system enforces role-based permissions so adjusters can view claims but only supervisors can approve payments above a threshold.

blocks.text: Control statement
Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.
Enhancements (13 active, 2 withdrawn)

rows: **AC-3(10)** Audited Override of Access Control Mechanisms
**AC-3(11)** Restrict Access to Specific Information Types

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-2, AC-4, AC-5, AC-6, AC-16, AC-17, AC-18, AC-19, AC-20, AC-21, AC-22, AC-24, AC-25, AT-2, AT-3, AU-9 and 28 more.
**Information Flow Enforcement.** Control how information flows within and between systems according to approved policies, for example between security domains or network zones.
blocks.practice: Information flow control regulates where information can travel within a system and between systems (in contrast to who is allowed to access the information) and without regard to subsequent accesses to that information.
blocks.example: A data diode lets telemetry flow from the OT network to the IT historian but blocks any traffic in the opposite direction.

blocks.text: Control statement
Enforce approved authorizations for controlling the flow of information within the system and between connected systems based on [Assignment: organization-defined information flow control policies].
Enhancements (30 active, 2 withdrawn)

rows: **AC-4(10)** Enable and Disable Security or Privacy Policy Filters
**AC-4(11)** Configuration of Security or Privacy Policy Filters
**AC-4(14)** Security or Privacy Policy Filter Constraints
**AC-4(21)** Physical or Logical Separation of Information Flows

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-3, AC-6, AC-16, AC-17, AC-19, AC-21, AU-10, CA-3, CA-9, CM-7, PL-9, PM-24, SA-17, SC-4, SC-7, SC-16 and 1 more.
**Separation of Duties.** Separate duties so no single person can misuse the system without collusion, and define access accordingly.
blocks.practice: Separation of duties addresses the potential for abuse of authorized privileges and helps to reduce the risk of malevolent activity without collusion.
blocks.example: Developers can push code but only the release team can deploy to production, and neither can approve their own change.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Identify and document [Assignment: organization-defined duties of individuals] ; and
**b.** Define system access authorizations to support separation of duties.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-2, AC-3, AC-6, AU-9, CM-5, CM-11, CP-9, IA-2, IA-4, IA-5, IA-12, MA-3, MA-5, PS-2, SA-8, SA-17.
**Least Privilege.** Give users and processes only the privileges they need to perform assigned tasks.
blocks.practice: Organizations employ least privilege for specific duties and systems. The principle of least privilege is also applied to system processes, ensuring that the processes have access to systems and operate at privilege levels no higher than necessary to accomplish organizational missions or business functions.
blocks.example: Administrators use just-in-time elevation through a PAM tool instead of holding standing domain admin rights.

blocks.text: Control statement
Employ the principle of least privilege, allowing only authorized accesses for users (or processes acting on behalf of users) that are necessary to accomplish assigned organizational tasks.
Enhancements (10 active)

rows: **AC-6(10)** Prohibit Non-privileged Users from Executing Privileged Functions

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-2, AC-3, AC-5, AC-16, CM-5, CM-11, PL-2, PM-12, SA-8, SA-15, SA-17, SC-38.
**Unsuccessful Logon Attempts.** Limit consecutive failed logon attempts and lock the account or delay further attempts when the limit is exceeded.
blocks.practice: The need to limit unsuccessful logon attempts and take subsequent action when the maximum number of attempts is exceeded applies regardless of whether the logon occurs via a local or network connection. Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period.
blocks.example: After five failed attempts in 15 minutes the VPN account is locked for 30 minutes and the SOC is alerted.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period] ; and

**b.** Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for [Assignment: organization-defined time period] ; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm] ; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action] ] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.

blocks.text: Enhancements (3 active, 1 withdrawn)
**Related controls:** AC-2, AC-9, AU-2, AU-6, IA-5.
**System Use Notification.** Show an approved system use notification before granting access, stating monitoring and acceptable use conditions.
blocks.practice: System use notifications can be implemented using messages or warning banners displayed before individuals log in to systems. System use notifications are used only for access via logon interfaces with human users. Notifications are not required when human interfaces do not exist.
blocks.example: Every server and the SSO login page display a banner stating that use is monitored and unauthorised use is prohibited.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Display [Assignment: organization-defined system use notification] to users before granting access to the system that provides privacy and security notices consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines and state that:
**a.1.** Users are accessing a U.S. Government system;
**a.2.** System usage may be monitored, recorded, and subject to audit;
**a.3.** Unauthorized use of the system is prohibited and subject to criminal and civil penalties; and
**a.4.** Use of the system indicates consent to monitoring and recording;
**b.** Retain the notification message or banner on the screen until users acknowledge the usage conditions and take explicit actions to log on to or further access the system; and
**c.** For publicly accessible systems:
**c.1.** Display system use information [Assignment: organization-defined conditions] , before granting further access to the publicly accessible system;
**c.2.** Display references, if any, to monitoring, recording, or auditing that are consistent with privacy accommodations for such systems that generally prohibit those activities; and
**c.3.** Include a description of the authorized uses of the system.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-14, PL-4, SI-4.
**Previous Logon Notification.** Tell users, on successful logon, the date and time of their last logon so they can spot unauthorised use.
blocks.practice: Previous logon notification is applicable to system access via human user interfaces and access to systems that occurs in other types of architectures. Information about the last successful logon allows the user to recognize if the date and time provided is not consistent with the user’s last access.
blocks.example: The banking admin portal shows "Last login: yesterday 18:42 from Port Louis" so staff notice sessions they didn't make.

blocks.text: Control statement
Notify the user, upon successful logon to the system, of the date and time of the last logon.
Enhancements (4 active)
**Related controls:** AC-7, PL-4.
**Concurrent Session Control.** Limit how many concurrent sessions an account or account type may have.
blocks.practice: Organizations may define the maximum number of concurrent sessions for system accounts globally, by account type, by account, or any combination thereof. For example, organizations may limit the number of concurrent sessions for system administrators or other individuals working in particularly sensitive domains or mission-critical applications.
blocks.example: Privileged accounts are limited to one active session at a time on the core banking system.

blocks.text: Control statement
Limit the number of concurrent sessions for each [Assignment: organization-defined account and/or account types] to [Assignment: organization-defined number].
**Related controls:** SC-23.
**Device Lock.** Lock the device after a period of inactivity or on user request, and keep the lock until the user re-authenticates.
blocks.practice: Device locks are temporary actions taken to prevent logical access to organizational systems when users stop work and move away from the immediate vicinity of those systems but do not want to log out because of the temporary nature of their absences. Device locks can be implemented at the operating system level or at the application level.
blocks.example: Workstations lock after 10 minutes idle, and users press Win+L when leaving their desk.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Prevent further access to the system by [Selection (one or more): initiating a device lock after [Assignment: organization-defined time period] of inactivity; requiring the user to initiate a device lock before leaving the system unattended] ; and
**b.** Retain the device lock until the user reestablishes access using established identification and authentication procedures.

blocks.text: Enhancements (1 active)
**Related controls:** AC-2, AC-7, IA-11, PL-4.
**Session Termination.** Automatically end user sessions after defined conditions, such as inactivity or time of day.
blocks.practice: Session termination addresses the termination of user-initiated logical sessions (in contrast to [SC-10](#sc-10) , which addresses the termination of network connections associated with communications sessions (i.e., network disconnect)). A logical session (for local, network, and remote access) is initiated whenever a user (or process acting on behalf of a user) accesses an organizational system.
blocks.example: The HR self-service portal ends sessions after 15 minutes of inactivity and forces re-login.

blocks.text: Control statement
Automatically terminate a user session after [Assignment: organization-defined conditions or trigger events].
Enhancements (3 active)
**Related controls:** MA-4, SC-10, SC-23.

sections.title: AC-14 Permitted Actions Without Identification or Authentication

blocks.text: **Permitted Actions Without Identification or Authentication.** Identify and document any actions users may take without identification or authentication, with justification.
blocks.practice: Specific user actions may be permitted without identification or authentication if organizations determine that identification and authentication are not required for the specified user actions.
blocks.example: Only the public website's read-only pages are available without login; this is documented in the system security plan.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Identify [Assignment: organization-defined user actions] that can be performed on the system without identification or authentication consistent with organizational mission and business functions; and
**b.** Document and provide supporting rationale in the security plan for the system, user actions not requiring identification or authentication.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-8, IA-2, PL-2.
**Security and Privacy Attributes.** Associate security and privacy attributes (labels such as classification or consent) with information and use them in access decisions.
blocks.practice: Information is represented internally within systems using abstractions known as data structures. Internal data structures can represent different types of entities, both active and passive. Active entities, also known as subjects, are typically associated with individuals, devices, or processes acting on behalf of individuals.
blocks.example: Documents carry sensitivity labels that the DLP and file-sharing platform read to block external sharing of Confidential files.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Provide the means to associate [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined types of security and privacy attributes] with [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined security and privacy attribute values] for information in storage, in process, and/or in transmission;
**b.** Ensure that the attribute associations are made and retained with the information;

**c.** Establish the following permitted security and privacy attributes from the attributes defined in [AC-16a](#ac-16_smt.a) for [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined systems]: [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined security and privacy attributes];
**d.** Determine the following permitted attribute values or ranges for each of the established attributes: [Assignment: organization-defined attribute values or ranges];
**e.** Audit changes to attributes; and
**f.** Review [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined security and privacy attributes] for applicability [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined frequency].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-3, AC-4, AC-6, AC-21, AC-25, AU-2, AU-10, MP-3, PE-22, PT-2, PT-3, PT-4, SC-11, SC-16, SI-12, SI-18.
**Remote Access.** Establish and authorise usage restrictions and configuration for each type of remote access before allowing it.
blocks.practice: Remote access is access to organizational systems (or processes acting on behalf of users) that communicate through external networks such as the Internet. Types of remote access include dial-up, broadband, and wireless. Organizations use encrypted virtual private networks (VPNs) to enhance confidentiality and integrity for remote connections.
blocks.example: Remote access is only through the managed ZTNA client with MFA; direct RDP from the internet is prohibited.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Establish and document usage restrictions, configuration/connection requirements, and implementation guidance for each type of remote access allowed; and
**b.** Authorize each type of remote access to the system prior to allowing such connections.

rows: **AC-17(2)** Protection of Confidentiality and Integrity Using Encryption

**Wireless Access.** Establish usage restrictions and configuration requirements for wireless access and authorise it before connection.
blocks.practice: Wireless technologies include microwave, packet radio (ultra-high frequency or very high frequency), 802.11x, and Bluetooth. Wireless networks use authentication protocols that provide authenticator protection and mutual authentication.
blocks.example: Corporate Wi-Fi uses WPA3-Enterprise with certificates; guest Wi-Fi is isolated from internal networks.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance for each type of wireless access; and
**b.** Authorize each type of wireless access to the system prior to allowing such connections.

sections.title: AC-19 Access Control for Mobile Devices

blocks.text: **Access Control for Mobile Devices.** Set configuration and connection requirements for mobile devices and authorise their connection to systems.
blocks.practice: A mobile device is a computing device that has a small form factor such that it can easily be carried by a single individual; is designed to operate without a physical connection; possesses local, non-removable or removable data storage; and includes a self-contained power source.
blocks.example: Only enrolled, compliant phones in the MDM can access corporate email and apps.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance for organization-controlled mobile devices, to include when such devices are outside of controlled areas; and
**b.** Authorize the connection of mobile devices to organizational systems.

**Data Mining Protection.** Protect data stores against unauthorised data mining.
blocks.practice: Data mining is an analytical process that attempts to find correlations or patterns in large data sets for the purpose of data or knowledge discovery. Data storage objects include database records and database fields. Sensitive information can be extracted from data mining operations.
blocks.example: A customer database limits query volumes and alerts on bulk extraction patterns typical of scraping.

**Access Control Decisions.** Ensure access control decisions are applied to each access request before enforcement.
blocks.practice: Access control decisions (also known as authorization decisions) occur when authorization information is applied to specific accesses. In contrast, access enforcement occurs when systems enforce access control decisions. While it is common to have access control decisions and access enforcement implemented by the same entity, it is not required, and it is not always an optimal implementation choice.
blocks.example: An API gateway queries a central policy decision point for every request before forwarding it.

A reference validation mechanism is always invoked, tamper-proof, and small enough to be subject to analysis and tests, the completeness of which can be assured (i.e., verifiable).
blocks.example: A hardened separation kernel mediates all access in a high-assurance cross-domain system.

blocks.practice: Audit and accountability policy and procedures address the controls in the AU family that are implemented within systems and organizations. **Event Logging.** Identify the types of events the system must log, coordinated with other functions, and review the list periodically.
blocks.practice: An event is an observable occurrence in a system. The types of events that require logging are those events that are significant and relevant to the security of systems and the privacy of individuals. Event logging also supports specific monitoring and auditing needs.
blocks.example: The event list includes logons, privilege changes, admin commands and access to customer records, chosen with the SOC and privacy office.

**c.** Specify the following event types for logging within the system: [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined event types (subset of the event types defined in [AU-2a.](#au-2_smt.a)) along with the frequency of (or situation requiring) logging for each identified event type];
**d.** Provide a rationale for why the event types selected for logging are deemed to be adequate to support after-the-fact investigations of incidents; and
**e.** Review and update the event types selected for logging [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].

**Content of Audit Records.** Make sure audit records contain enough information: what happened, when, where, source, outcome and identity.
blocks.practice: Audit record content that may be necessary to support the auditing function includes event descriptions (item a), time stamps (item b), source and destination addresses (item c), user or process identifiers (items d and f), success or fail indications (item e), and filenames involved (items a, c, e, and f) .
blocks.example: Application logs include user ID, timestamp, source IP, action, record ID and success or failure.

blocks.text: Control statement
Ensure that audit records contain information that establishes the following:

items: **a.** What type of event occurred;
**b.** When the event occurred;
**c.** Where the event occurred;
**d.** Source of the event;
**e.** Outcome of the event; and
**f.** Identity of any individuals, subjects, or objects/entities associated with the event.

**Audit Log Storage Capacity.** Allocate enough audit log storage to meet retention requirements and reduce the chance of capacity being exceeded.
blocks.practice: Organizations consider the types of audit logging to be performed and the audit log processing requirements when allocating audit log storage capacity. Allocating sufficient audit log storage capacity reduces the likelihood of such capacity being exceeded and resulting in the potential loss or reduction of audit logging capability.
blocks.example: Log storage is sized for 13 months with alerts at 80% capacity.

sections.title: AU-5 Response to Audit Logging Process Failures

blocks.text: **Response to Audit Logging Process Failures.** Alert defined staff when audit logging fails and take defined actions, such as shutting down or overwriting oldest records.
blocks.practice: Audit logging process failures include software and hardware errors, failures in audit log capturing mechanisms, and reaching or exceeding audit log storage capacity. Organization-defined actions include overwriting oldest audit records, shutting down the system, and stopping the generation of audit records.
blocks.example: The SIEM alerts the on-call engineer when a Tier 1 server stops sending logs for 15 minutes.

items: **a.** Alert [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] within [Assignment: organization-defined time period] in the event of an audit logging process failure; and

sections.title: AU-6 Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting

blocks.text: **Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting.** Review and analyse audit records for signs of inappropriate or unusual activity and report findings.
blocks.practice: Audit record review, analysis, and reporting covers information security- and privacy-related logging performed by organizations, including logging that results from the monitoring of account usage, remote access, wireless connectivity, mobile device connection, configuration settings, system component inventory, use of maintenance tools and non-local maintenance, physical access, temperature and humidity, equipment delivery and removal, communications at system interfaces, and use of mobile code or Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP).
blocks.example: SOC analysts review correlated alerts daily and escalate suspicious admin activity to the incident team.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Review and analyze system audit records [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] for indications of [Assignment: organization-defined inappropriate or unusual activity] and the potential impact of the inappropriate or unusual activity;
**b.** Report findings to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] ; and

**c.** Adjust the level of audit record review, analysis, and reporting within the system when there is a change in risk based on law enforcement information, intelligence information, or other credible sources of information.

sections.title: AU-7 Audit Record Reduction and Report Generation

blocks.text: **Audit Record Reduction and Report Generation.** Provide audit record reduction and report generation that supports review and investigations without altering original records.
blocks.practice: Audit record reduction is a process that manipulates collected audit log information and organizes it into a summary format that is more meaningful to analysts. Audit record reduction and report generation capabilities do not always emanate from the same system or from the same organizational entities that conduct audit logging activities.
blocks.example: Investigators can filter a year of logs by user and time in the SIEM without modifying stored records.

blocks.text: Control statement
Provide and implement an audit record reduction and report generation capability that:

items: **a.** Supports on-demand audit record review, analysis, and reporting requirements and after-the-fact investigations of incidents; and
**b.** Does not alter the original content or time ordering of audit records.

**Time Stamps.** Use internal system clocks to generate time stamps and record them in a consistent time format (e.g. UTC).
blocks.practice: Time stamps generated by the system include date and time. Time is commonly expressed in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), a modern continuation of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), or local time with an offset from UTC. Granularity of time measurements refers to the degree of synchronization between system clocks and reference clocks (e.g., clocks synchronizing within hundreds of milliseconds or tens of milliseconds).
blocks.example: All systems sync to internal NTP servers and log in UTC to support correlation.

items: **a.** Use internal system clocks to generate time stamps for audit records; and

**b.** Record time stamps for audit records that meet [Assignment: organization-defined granularity of time measurement] and that use Coordinated Universal Time, have a fixed local time offset from Coordinated Universal Time, or that include the local time offset as part of the time stamp.

**Protection of Audit Information.** Protect audit information and tools from unauthorised access, modification and deletion.
blocks.practice: Audit information includes all information needed to successfully audit system activity, such as audit records, audit log settings, audit reports, and personally identifiable information. Audit logging tools are those programs and devices used to conduct system audit and logging activities.

**Control Assessments.** Plan and conduct control assessments with an appropriate team, and report results to stakeholders.

blocks.text: **Plan of Action and Milestones.** Develop and update a plan of action and milestones (POA&M) for weaknesses found in assessments and monitoring.
blocks.practice: Plans of action and milestones are useful for any type of organization to track planned remedial actions. Plans of action and milestones are required in authorization packages and subject to federal reporting requirements established by OMB.

**Authorization.** Assign a senior official to authorise the system to operate (and common controls), accepting the residual risk, and update authorisations periodically.
blocks.practice: Authorizations are official management decisions by senior officials to authorize operation of systems, authorize the use of common controls for inheritance by organizational systems, and explicitly accept the risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation based on the implementation of agreed-upon controls.
blocks.example: The COO signs the authorisation to operate after reviewing the security plan, assessment report and POA&M.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Assign a senior official as the authorizing official for the system;
**b.** Assign a senior official as the authorizing official for common controls available for inheritance by organizational systems;

**c.1.** Accepts the use of common controls inherited by the system; and
**c.2.** Authorizes the system to operate;
**d.** Ensure that the authorizing official for common controls authorizes the use of those controls for inheritance by organizational systems;
**e.** Update the authorizations [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].

**Continuous Monitoring.** Develop and run a continuous monitoring strategy with defined metrics, frequencies, analysis and reporting.
blocks.practice: Continuous monitoring at the system level facilitates ongoing awareness of the system security and privacy posture to support organizational risk management decisions. The terms "continuous" and "ongoing" imply that organizations assess and monitor their controls and risks at a frequency sufficient to support risk-based decisions. Different types of controls may require different monitoring frequencies.
blocks.example: Dashboards track patch compliance, configuration drift and open POA&Ms weekly, reported monthly to the authorising official.

blocks.text: Control statement
Develop a system-level continuous monitoring strategy and implement continuous monitoring in accordance with the organization-level continuous monitoring strategy that includes:

items: **a.** Establishing the following system-level metrics to be monitored: [Assignment: organization-defined system-level metrics];
**b.** Establishing [Assignment: organization-defined frequencies] for monitoring and [Assignment: organization-defined frequencies] for assessment of control effectiveness;
**c.** Ongoing control assessments in accordance with the continuous monitoring strategy;
**d.** Ongoing monitoring of system and organization-defined metrics in accordance with the continuous monitoring strategy;
**e.** Correlation and analysis of information generated by control assessments and monitoring;
**f.** Response actions to address results of the analysis of control assessment and monitoring information; and

**g.** Reporting the security and privacy status of the system to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined personnel or roles] [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined frequency].

**Penetration Testing.** Conduct penetration testing on defined systems at a defined frequency.
blocks.practice: Penetration testing is a specialized type of assessment conducted on systems or individual system components to identify vulnerabilities that could be exploited by adversaries. Penetration testing goes beyond automated vulnerability scanning and is conducted by agents and teams with demonstrable skills and experience that include technical expertise in network, operating system, and/or application level security.
blocks.example: Annual external and internal penetration tests are run on the high-impact payment platform.

**Configuration Change Control.** Control changes to the system: propose, review, approve, test, implement and document them, including security and privacy impact.
blocks.practice: Configuration change control for organizational systems involves the systematic proposal, justification, implementation, testing, review, and disposition of system changes, including system upgrades and modifications.
blocks.example: A change advisory board reviews significant changes; standard changes are pre-approved and automated.

blocks.text: Control statement

**b.** Review proposed configuration-controlled changes to the system and approve or disapprove such changes with explicit consideration for security and privacy impact analyses;

**d.** Implement approved configuration-controlled changes to the system;
**e.** Retain records of configuration-controlled changes to the system for [Assignment: organization-defined time period];
**f.** Monitor and review activities associated with configuration-controlled changes to the system; and

**g.** Coordinate and provide oversight for configuration change control activities through [Assignment: organization-defined configuration change control element] that convenes [Selection (one or more): [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] ; when [Assignment: organization-defined configuration change conditions] ].

blocks.practice: Organizational personnel with security or privacy responsibilities conduct impact analyses. Individuals conducting impact analyses possess the necessary skills and technical expertise to analyze the changes to systems as well as the security or privacy ramifications.

blocks.practice: Changes to the hardware, software, or firmware components of systems or the operational procedures related to the system can potentially have significant effects on the security of the systems or individuals’ privacy. Therefore, organizations permit only qualified and authorized individuals to access systems for purposes of initiating changes.
blocks.example: Only the deployment pipeline service account can change production; engineers have no direct write access.

**Configuration Settings.** Establish and document mandatory configuration settings using secure baselines, implement them and monitor deviations.
blocks.practice: Configuration settings are the parameters that can be changed in the hardware, software, or firmware components of the system that affect the security and privacy posture or functionality of the system. Information technology products for which configuration settings can be defined include mainframe computers, servers, workstations, operating systems, mobile devices, input/output devices, protocols, and applications.
blocks.example: Servers are hardened to CIS Level 1 Benchmarks, with deviations documented and drift reported weekly.

**b.** Implement the configuration settings;

**c.** Identify, document, and approve any deviations from established configuration settings for [Assignment: organization-defined system components] based on [Assignment: organization-defined operational requirements] ; and
**d.** Monitor and control changes to the configuration settings in accordance with organizational policies and procedures.

**Least Functionality.** Configure the system to provide only essential capabilities, prohibiting or restricting unneeded functions, ports, protocols and services.
blocks.practice: Systems provide a wide variety of functions and services. Some of the functions and services routinely provided by default may not be necessary to support essential organizational missions, functions, or operations. Additionally, it is sometimes convenient to provide multiple services from a single system component, but doing so increases risk over limiting the services provided by that single component.
blocks.example: Web servers run only the HTTPS service; Telnet, FTP and unused modules are disabled.

**System Component Inventory.** Develop and maintain an accurate, complete inventory of system components at the level needed for tracking and reporting.
blocks.practice: System components are discrete, identifiable information technology assets that include hardware, software, and firmware. Organizations may choose to implement centralized system component inventories that include components from all organizational systems. In such situations, organizations ensure that the inventories include system-specific information required for component accountability.
blocks.example: The CMDB is populated automatically from discovery tools and reconciled monthly with the asset register.

**a.4.** Is at the level of granularity deemed necessary for tracking and reporting; and

**Configuration Management Plan.** Develop and implement a configuration management plan defining roles, processes and configuration items.
blocks.practice: Configuration management activities occur throughout the system development life cycle. As such, there are developmental configuration management activities (e.g., the control of code and software libraries) and operational configuration management activities (e.g., control of installed components and how the components are configured).
blocks.example: The CM plan for the ERP defines configuration items, the change board, and how baselines are versioned.

items: **a.** Addresses roles, responsibilities, and configuration management processes and procedures;
**b.** Establishes a process for identifying configuration items throughout the system development life cycle and for managing the configuration of the configuration items;
**c.** Defines the configuration items for the system and places the configuration items under configuration management;

blocks.practice: Information location addresses the need to understand where information is being processed and stored. Information location includes identifying where specific information types and information reside in system components and how information is being processed so that information flow can be understood and adequate protection and policy management provided for such information and system components.

blocks.practice: Contingency planning policy and procedures address the controls in the CP family that are implemented within systems and organizations. The risk management strategy is an important factor in establishing such policies and procedures. Policies and procedures contribute to security and privacy assurance.
blocks.example: The continuity manager owns the contingency planning policy, reviewed after each annual exercise.

items: **a.** Develop, document, and disseminate to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined personnel or roles]:
**a.1.** [Selection (one or more): organization-level; mission/business process-level; system-level] contingency planning policy that:
**a.1.(a).** Addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; and
**a.1.(b).** Is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; and
**a.2.** Procedures to facilitate the implementation of the contingency planning policy and the associated contingency planning controls;
**b.** Designate an [Assignment: organization-defined official] to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the contingency planning policy and procedures; and
**c.** Review and update the current contingency planning:
**c.1.** Policy [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events] ; and

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PM-9, PS-8, SI-12.
**Contingency Plan.** Develop, approve, distribute and maintain a contingency plan covering essential functions, recovery objectives, roles, and restoration.
blocks.practice: Contingency planning for systems is part of an overall program for achieving continuity of operations for organizational mission and business functions. Contingency planning addresses system restoration and implementation of alternative mission or business processes when systems are compromised or breached.
blocks.example: The core banking contingency plan defines a 4-hour RTO, key contacts and step-by-step failover procedures.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop a contingency plan for the system that:
**a.1.** Identifies essential mission and business functions and associated contingency requirements;
**a.2.** Provides recovery objectives, restoration priorities, and metrics;
**a.3.** Addresses contingency roles, responsibilities, assigned individuals with contact information;
**a.4.** Addresses maintaining essential mission and business functions despite a system disruption, compromise, or failure;
**a.5.** Addresses eventual, full system restoration without deterioration of the controls originally planned and implemented;
**a.6.** Addresses the sharing of contingency information; and
**a.7.** Is reviewed and approved by [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined personnel or roles];
**b.** Distribute copies of the contingency plan to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined key contingency personnel (identified by name and/or by role) and organizational elements];
**c.** Coordinate contingency planning activities with incident handling activities;
**d.** Review the contingency plan for the system [Assignment: organization-defined frequency];
**e.** Update the contingency plan to address changes to the organization, system, or environment of operation and problems encountered during contingency plan implementation, execution, or testing;
**f.** Communicate contingency plan changes to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined key contingency personnel (identified by name and/or by role) and organizational elements];
**g.** Incorporate lessons learned from contingency plan testing, training, or actual contingency activities into contingency testing and training; and
**h.** Protect the contingency plan from unauthorized disclosure and modification.

**Alternate Storage Site.** Establish an alternate storage site for backups with agreements to store and retrieve them.
blocks.practice: Alternate storage sites are geographically distinct from primary storage sites and maintain duplicate copies of information and data if the primary storage site is not available. Similarly, alternate processing sites provide processing capability if the primary processing site is not available. Geographically distributed architectures that support contingency requirements may be considered alternate storage sites.
blocks.example: Encrypted backups are replicated to a second cloud region operated under the same contract.

**Alternate Processing Site.** Establish an alternate processing site so essential functions can resume within recovery time objectives.
blocks.practice: Alternate processing sites are geographically distinct from primary processing sites and provide processing capability if the primary processing site is not available. The alternate processing capability may be addressed using a physical processing site or other alternatives, such as failover to a cloud-based service provider or other internally or externally provided processing service.
blocks.example: A warm site in another city can run the claims system within 24 hours of a primary site loss.

blocks.practice: System-level information includes system state information, operating system software, middleware, application software, and licenses. User-level information includes information other than system-level information. Mechanisms employed to protect the integrity of system backups include digital signatures and cryptographic hashes.
blocks.example: Nightly backups are encrypted, copied to immutable storage and restore-tested quarterly.

**System Recovery and Reconstitution.** Provide for recovery and reconstitution of the system to a known state within defined time after disruption.
blocks.practice: Recovery is executing contingency plan activities to restore organizational mission and business functions. Reconstitution takes place following recovery and includes activities for returning systems to fully operational states.
blocks.example: Rebuild scripts restore servers from hardened images and data from backups to a verified clean state.

**Alternate Communications Protocols.** Provide the ability to use alternate communications protocols to support continuity.
blocks.practice: Contingency plans and the contingency training or testing associated with those plans incorporate an alternate communications protocol capability as part of establishing resilience in organizational systems. Switching communications protocols may affect software applications and operational aspects of systems.
blocks.example: If the primary VPN protocol is disrupted, sites can fail over to a secondary protocol and provider.

**Safe Mode.** When defined conditions are detected, enter a safe mode of operation with restricted functions.
blocks.practice: For systems that support critical mission and business functions—including military operations, civilian space operations, nuclear power plant operations, and air traffic control operations (especially real-time operational environments)—organizations can identify certain conditions under which those systems revert to a predefined safe mode of operation.
blocks.example: An industrial controller drops into a safe state that stops the process if sensor readings become inconsistent.

**Alternative Security Mechanisms.** Use alternative or supplemental security mechanisms when primary means are compromised.
blocks.practice: Use of alternative security mechanisms supports system resiliency, contingency planning, and continuity of operations. To ensure mission and business continuity, organizations can implement alternative or supplemental security mechanisms. The mechanisms may be less effective than the primary mechanisms.
blocks.example: If the MFA provider is down, a break-glass process with hardware tokens and extra approvals is used.

blocks.text: Identification and Authentication makes sure users, devices and services are uniquely identified and properly authenticated, with strong management of identifiers and authenticators.

blocks.text: IA-2 base control requires unique identification and authentication; MFA for privileged and non-privileged accounts comes through IA-2(1) and IA-2(2), which are in all three security baselines.
**Policy and Procedures.** Maintain an identification and authentication policy and procedures, owned and reviewed on schedule.
blocks.practice: Identification and authentication policy and procedures address the controls in the IA family that are implemented within systems and organizations. The risk management strategy is an important factor in establishing such policies and procedures. Policies and procedures contribute to security and privacy assurance.
blocks.example: The IAM team owns the authentication standard defining MFA, password and certificate requirements.

**a.1.** [Selection (one or more): organization-level; mission/business process-level; system-level] identification and authentication policy that:
**a.1.(a).** Addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; and
**a.1.(b).** Is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; and
**a.2.** Procedures to facilitate the implementation of the identification and authentication policy and the associated identification and authentication controls;
**b.** Designate an [Assignment: organization-defined official] to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the identification and authentication policy and procedures; and

**Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users).** Uniquely identify and authenticate organisational users and processes acting for them. Enhancements add MFA and replay resistance.
blocks.practice: Organizations can satisfy the identification and authentication requirements by complying with the requirements in [HSPD 12](#f16e438e-7114-4144-bfe2-2dfcad8cb2d0) . Organizational users include employees or individuals who organizations consider to have an equivalent status to employees (e.g., contractors and guest researchers).
blocks.example: All staff sign in through the corporate identity provider with MFA; shared accounts are prohibited.

blocks.text: Control statement
Uniquely identify and authenticate organizational users and associate that unique identification with processes acting on behalf of those users.

**Device Identification and Authentication.** Uniquely identify and authenticate devices before establishing connections.
blocks.practice: Devices that require unique device-to-device identification and authentication are defined by type, device, or a combination of type and device. Organization-defined device types include devices that are not owned by the organization.
blocks.example: Only devices with a valid company certificate can join the internal network through 802.1X.

**Identifier Management.** Manage identifiers: authorise assignment, select unique identifiers, and prevent reuse for a defined period.
blocks.practice: Common device identifiers include Media Access Control (MAC) addresses, Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, or device-unique token identifiers. The management of individual identifiers is not applicable to shared system accounts. Typically, individual identifiers are the usernames of the system accounts assigned to those individuals.
blocks.example: Usernames are never reused after an employee leaves, so old logs remain attributable.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Receiving authorization from [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] to assign an individual, group, role, service, or device identifier;
**b.** Selecting an identifier that identifies an individual, group, role, service, or device;
**c.** Assigning the identifier to the intended individual, group, role, service, or device; and
**d.** Preventing reuse of identifiers for [Assignment: organization-defined time period].

**Authenticator Management.** Manage authenticators (passwords, tokens, certificates, keys): initial distribution, strength, protection, changes and revocation.
blocks.practice: Authenticators include passwords, cryptographic devices, biometrics, certificates, one-time password devices, and ID badges. Device authenticators include certificates and passwords. Initial authenticator content is the actual content of the authenticator (e.g., the initial password). In contrast, the requirements for authenticator content contain specific criteria or characteristics (e.g., minimum password length).
blocks.example: Passwords follow SP 800-63B guidance, are checked against breached lists, and hardware tokens are revoked on loss.

blocks.text: Control statement
Manage system authenticators by:

items: **a.** Verifying, as part of the initial authenticator distribution, the identity of the individual, group, role, service, or device receiving the authenticator;
**b.** Establishing initial authenticator content for any authenticators issued by the organization;
**c.** Ensuring that authenticators have sufficient strength of mechanism for their intended use;
**d.** Establishing and implementing administrative procedures for initial authenticator distribution, for lost or compromised or damaged authenticators, and for revoking authenticators;
**e.** Changing default authenticators prior to first use;
**f.** Changing or refreshing authenticators [Assignment: organization-defined time period by authenticator type] or when [Assignment: organization-defined events] occur;
**g.** Protecting authenticator content from unauthorized disclosure and modification;
**h.** Requiring individuals to take, and having devices implement, specific controls to protect authenticators; and
**i.** Changing authenticators for group or role accounts when membership to those accounts changes.

**Authentication Feedback.** Obscure authentication feedback so it can't be exploited, for example by masking passwords.
blocks.practice: Authentication feedback from systems does not provide information that would allow unauthorized individuals to compromise authentication mechanisms. For some types of systems, such as desktops or notebooks with relatively large monitors, the threat (referred to as shoulder surfing) may be significant.
blocks.example: Password fields show dots, and failed login messages don't say whether the username or password was wrong.

**Cryptographic Module Authentication.** Use authentication mechanisms for cryptographic modules that meet applicable requirements.
blocks.practice: Authentication mechanisms may be required within a cryptographic module to authenticate an operator accessing the module and to verify that the operator is authorized to assume the requested role and perform services within that role.
blocks.example: Administrators of the HSM authenticate with smart cards as required by its FIPS 140 validation.

blocks.practice: Non-organizational users include system users other than organizational users explicitly covered by [IA-2](#ia-2) . Non-organizational users are uniquely identified and authenticated for accesses other than those explicitly identified and documented in [AC-14](#ac-14) .
blocks.example: Customers log into internet banking with individual accounts and MFA; partners use federated identities.

**Service Identification and Authentication.** Uniquely identify and authenticate services before establishing communications with them.
blocks.practice: Services that may require identification and authentication include web applications using digital certificates or services or applications that query a database. Identification and authentication methods for system services and applications include information or code signing, provenance graphs, and electronic signatures that indicate the sources of services.
blocks.example: Microservices authenticate to each other with mutual TLS certificates issued by an internal CA.

**Adaptive Authentication.** Require individuals to provide additional authentication in defined high-risk situations (adaptive authentication).
blocks.practice: Adversaries may compromise individual authentication mechanisms employed by organizations and subsequently attempt to impersonate legitimate users. To address this threat, organizations may employ specific techniques or mechanisms and establish protocols to assess suspicious behavior.
blocks.example: A login from a new country triggers step-up authentication with a hardware key.

**Related controls:** IA-2, IA-8.
**Re-authentication.** Require users to re-authenticate in defined circumstances.
blocks.practice: In addition to the re-authentication requirements associated with device locks, organizations may require re-authentication of individuals in certain situations, including when roles, authenticators or credentials change, when security categories of systems change, when the execution of privileged functions occurs, after a fixed time period, or periodically.
blocks.example: Users must re-enter MFA before changing bank details or approving large payments.

blocks.text: Control statement
Require users to re-authenticate when [Assignment: organization-defined circumstances or situations].
**Related controls:** AC-3, AC-11, IA-2, IA-3, IA-4, IA-8.
**Identity Proofing.** Identity-proof users who need accounts, based on assurance level requirements (SP 800-63A).
blocks.practice: Identity proofing is the process of collecting, validating, and verifying a user’s identity information for the purposes of establishing credentials for accessing a system. Identity proofing is intended to mitigate threats to the registration of users and the establishment of their accounts.
blocks.example: New contractors present government ID verified in person before receiving accounts to sensitive systems.

items: **a.** Identity proof users that require accounts for logical access to systems based on appropriate identity assurance level requirements as specified in applicable standards and guidelines;
**b.** Resolve user identities to a unique individual; and
**c.** Collect, validate, and verify identity evidence.

sections.title: IA-13 Identity Providers and Authorization Servers

blocks.text: **Identity Providers and Authorization Servers.** Use identity providers and authorisation servers to manage identities, attributes and access rights.
blocks.practice: Identity providers, both internal and external to the organization, manage the user, device, and NPE authenticators and issue statements, often called identity assertions, attesting to identities of other systems or systems components. **Incident Response Testing.** Test the incident response capability using defined tests at a defined frequency.
blocks.practice: Organizations test incident response capabilities to determine their effectiveness and identify potential weaknesses or deficiencies. Incident response testing includes the use of checklists, walk-through or tabletop exercises, and simulations (parallel or full interrupt).
blocks.example: A yearly ransomware tabletop with executives tests decision-making and communications.

**Incident Handling.** Implement incident handling covering preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication and recovery, coordinated with contingency planning.
blocks.practice: Organizations recognize that incident response capabilities are dependent on the capabilities of organizational systems and the mission and business processes being supported by those systems. Organizations consider incident response as part of the definition, design, and development of mission and business processes and systems.
blocks.example: Playbooks guide analysts from alert triage through isolation, eradication and restoration.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Implement an incident handling capability for incidents that is consistent with the incident response plan and includes preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery;
**b.** Coordinate incident handling activities with contingency planning activities;
**c.** Incorporate lessons learned from ongoing incident handling activities into incident response procedures, training, and testing, and implement the resulting changes accordingly; and
**d.** Ensure the rigor, intensity, scope, and results of incident handling activities are comparable and predictable across the organization.

**Incident Monitoring.** Track and document incidents.
blocks.practice: Documenting incidents includes maintaining records about each incident, the status of the incident, and other pertinent information necessary for forensics as well as evaluating incident details, trends, and handling.
blocks.example: Every incident is recorded in a case management system with timeline, actions and evidence.

**Incident Reporting.** Require personnel to report suspected incidents within a defined time and report incident information to defined authorities.
blocks.practice: The types of incidents reported, the content and timeliness of the reports, and the designated reporting authorities reflect applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines. Incident information can inform risk assessments, control effectiveness assessments, security requirements for acquisitions, and selection criteria for technology products.
blocks.example: Staff report suspected incidents within one hour; confirmed breaches go to the regulator within the legal deadline.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Require personnel to report suspected incidents to the organizational incident response capability within [Assignment: organization-defined time period] ; and
**b.** Report incident information to [Assignment: organization-defined authorities].

**Related controls:** CM-6, CP-2, IR-4, IR-5, IR-8, IR-9.
**Incident Response Assistance.** Provide an incident response support resource that offers advice and assistance to users.
blocks.practice: Incident response support resources provided by organizations include help desks, assistance groups, automated ticketing systems to open and track incident response tickets, and access to forensics services or consumer redress services, when required.
blocks.example: A 24x7 security hotline and help desk queue helps users handle suspected phishing and lost devices.

blocks.text: Control statement

**Incident Response Plan.** Develop, approve and maintain an incident response plan that provides a roadmap for the capability.
blocks.practice: It is important that organizations develop and implement a coordinated approach to incident response. Organizational mission and business functions determine the structure of incident response capabilities.
blocks.example: The IR plan defines roles, severity levels, communications and metrics, and is updated after each major incident.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop an incident response plan that:
**a.1.** Provides the organization with a roadmap for implementing its incident response capability;
**a.2.** Describes the structure and organization of the incident response capability;
**a.3.** Provides a high-level approach for how the incident response capability fits into the overall organization;
**a.4.** Meets the unique requirements of the organization, which relate to mission, size, structure, and functions;
**a.5.** Defines reportable incidents;
**a.6.** Provides metrics for measuring the incident response capability within the organization;
**a.7.** Defines the resources and management support needed to effectively maintain and mature an incident response capability;
**a.8.** Addresses the sharing of incident information;
**a.9.** Is reviewed and approved by [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] ; and
**a.10.** Explicitly designates responsibility for incident response to [Assignment: organization-defined entities, personnel, or roles].
**b.** Distribute copies of the incident response plan to [Assignment: organization-defined incident response personnel];
**c.** Update the incident response plan to address system and organizational changes or problems encountered during plan implementation, execution, or testing;

**d.** Communicate incident response plan changes to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined incident response personnel (identified by name and/or by role) and organizational elements] ; and
**e.** Protect the incident response plan from unauthorized disclosure and modification.

**Information Spillage Response.** Respond to information spills: identify the information, alert personnel, isolate and eradicate it, and identify other affected systems.
blocks.practice: Information spillage refers to instances where information is placed on systems that are not authorized to process such information. Information spills occur when information that is thought to be a certain classification or impact level is transmitted to a system and subsequently is determined to be of a higher classification or impact level. At that point, corrective action is required.
blocks.example: Classified data accidentally emailed to an unclassified system is located, deleted from all mailboxes and backups, and reported.

**d.** Isolating the contaminated system or system component;
**e.** Eradicating the information from the contaminated system or component;
**f.** Identifying other systems or system components that may have been subsequently contaminated; and
**g.** Performing the following additional actions: [Assignment: organization-defined actions].

blocks.text: Maintenance controls how systems are maintained: scheduled and controlled maintenance, tools, remote (nonlocal) maintenance, maintenance personnel and timely maintenance.

blocks.title: Remote maintenance is a common entry point
blocks.text: Vendor remote support tools are a frequent attack path. MA-4 requires strong authentication, logging and termination of nonlocal maintenance sessions.
**Policy and Procedures.** Maintain a system maintenance policy and procedures, owned and reviewed on schedule.
blocks.practice: Maintenance policy and procedures address the controls in the MA family that are implemented within systems and organizations. The risk management strategy is an important factor in establishing such policies and procedures. Policies and procedures contribute to security and privacy assurance.
blocks.example: IT operations maintains the maintenance policy covering vendor access and scheduled maintenance windows.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop, document, and disseminate to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined personnel or roles]:
**a.1.** [Selection (one or more): organization-level; mission/business process-level; system-level] maintenance policy that:
**a.1.(a).** Addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; and
**a.1.(b).** Is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; and
**a.2.** Procedures to facilitate the implementation of the maintenance policy and the associated maintenance controls;
**b.** Designate an [Assignment: organization-defined official] to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the maintenance policy and procedures; and
**c.** Review and update the current maintenance:
**c.1.** Policy [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events] ; and
**c.2.** Procedures [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PM-9, PS-8, SI-12.
**Controlled Maintenance.** Schedule, document and review maintenance and repairs, approve and monitor them, and verify controls afterwards.
blocks.practice: Controlling system maintenance addresses the information security aspects of the system maintenance program and applies to all types of maintenance to system components conducted by local or nonlocal entities. Maintenance includes peripherals such as scanners, copiers, and printers.
blocks.example: Hardware repairs are logged, approved and followed by a check that security settings are intact.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Schedule, document, and review records of maintenance, repair, and replacement on system components in accordance with manufacturer or vendor specifications and/or organizational requirements;
**b.** Approve and monitor all maintenance activities, whether performed on site or remotely and whether the system or system components are serviced on site or removed to another location;

**c.** Require that [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] explicitly approve the removal of the system or system components from organizational facilities for off-site maintenance, repair, or replacement;

**d.** Sanitize equipment to remove the following information from associated media prior to removal from organizational facilities for off-site maintenance, repair, or replacement: [Assignment: organization-defined information];
**e.** Check all potentially impacted controls to verify that the controls are still functioning properly following maintenance, repair, or replacement actions; and
**f.** Include the following information in organizational maintenance records: [Assignment: organization-defined information].

**Related controls:** CM-2, CM-3, CM-4, CM-5, CM-8, MA-4, MP-6, PE-16, SI-2, SR-3, SR-4, SR-11.
**Maintenance Tools.** Approve, control and monitor the use of system maintenance tools.
blocks.practice: Approving, controlling, monitoring, and reviewing maintenance tools address security-related issues associated with maintenance tools that are not within system authorization boundaries and are used specifically for diagnostic and repair actions on organizational systems. Organizations have flexibility in determining roles for the approval of maintenance tools and how that approval is documented.
blocks.example: Diagnostic tools brought by vendors are scanned and must be approved before connecting to production.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Approve, control, and monitor the use of system maintenance tools; and
**b.** Review previously approved system maintenance tools [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].

blocks.text: Enhancements (6 active)
**Related controls:** MA-2, PE-16.
**Nonlocal Maintenance.** Approve and monitor nonlocal (remote) maintenance, use strong authentication, keep records and terminate sessions when done.
blocks.practice: Nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic activities are conducted by individuals who communicate through either an external or internal network. Local maintenance and diagnostic activities are carried out by individuals who are physically present at the system location and not communicating across a network connection.
blocks.example: Vendor remote support goes through a PAM gateway with MFA, session recording and automatic termination.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Approve and monitor nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic activities;
**b.** Allow the use of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic tools only as consistent with organizational policy and documented in the security plan for the system;
**c.** Employ strong authentication in the establishment of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions;
**d.** Maintain records for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic activities; and
**e.** Terminate session and network connections when nonlocal maintenance is completed.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-2, AC-3, AC-6, AC-17, AU-2, AU-3, IA-2, IA-4, IA-5, IA-8, MA-2, MA-5, PL-2, SC-7, SC-10.
**Maintenance Personnel.** Authorise maintenance personnel and supervise those without required access authorisations.
blocks.practice: Maintenance personnel refers to individuals who perform hardware or software maintenance on organizational systems, while [PE-2](#pe-2) addresses physical access for individuals whose maintenance duties place them within the physical protection perimeter of the systems.
blocks.example: An escort supervises the HVAC contractor working in the data centre.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Establish a process for maintenance personnel authorization and maintain a list of authorized maintenance organizations or personnel;
**b.** Verify that non-escorted personnel performing maintenance on the system possess the required access authorizations; and

**c.** Designate organizational personnel with required access authorizations and technical competence to supervise the maintenance activities of personnel who do not possess the required access authorizations.

**Related controls:** AC-2, AC-3, AC-5, AC-6, IA-2, IA-8, MA-4, MP-2, PE-2, PE-3, PS-7, RA-3.
**Timely Maintenance.** Obtain maintenance support and spare parts within a defined time after failure.
blocks.practice: Organizations specify the system components that result in increased risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, or the Nation when the functionality provided by those components is not operational. Organizational actions to obtain maintenance support include having appropriate contracts in place.
blocks.example: Support contracts guarantee replacement parts for critical storage arrays within four hours.

blocks.text: Control statement
Obtain maintenance support and/or spare parts for [Assignment: organization-defined system components] within [Assignment: organization-defined time period] of failure.
