**Related controls:** CM-8, CP-2, CP-7, RA-7, SA-15, SI-13, SR-2, SR-3, SR-4.
**Field Maintenance.** Restrict or prohibit field maintenance on defined systems to trusted facilities.
blocks.practice: Field maintenance is the type of maintenance conducted on a system or system component after the system or component has been deployed to a specific site (i.e., operational environment). In certain instances, field maintenance (i.e., local maintenance at the site) may not be executed with the same degree of rigor or with the same quality control checks as depot maintenance.
blocks.example: Classified laptops are repaired only at an accredited depot, never by local repair shops.

**Related controls:** MA-2, MA-4, MA-5.

blocks.text: Media Protection covers access to, marking, storage, transport, sanitisation and use of digital and non-digital media.

blocks.title: Sanitisation guidance
blocks.text: Use NIST SP 800-88 for media sanitisation methods (clear, purge, destroy) to meet MP-6.
**Policy and Procedures.** Maintain a media protection policy and procedures, owned and reviewed on schedule.
blocks.practice: Media protection policy and procedures address the controls in the MP family that are implemented within systems and organizations. The risk management strategy is an important factor in establishing such policies and procedures. Policies and procedures contribute to security and privacy assurance.
blocks.example: The media policy covers USB use, encryption and disposal, reviewed annually.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop, document, and disseminate to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined personnel or roles]:
**a.1.** [Selection (one or more): organization-level; mission/business process-level; system-level] media protection policy that:
**a.1.(a).** Addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; and
**a.1.(b).** Is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; and
**a.2.** Procedures to facilitate the implementation of the media protection policy and the associated media protection controls;
**b.** Designate an [Assignment: organization-defined official] to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the media protection policy and procedures; and

**c.1.** Policy [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events] ; and
**c.2.** Procedures [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PM-9, PS-8, SI-12.
**Media Access.** Restrict access to defined types of digital and non-digital media to authorised individuals.
blocks.practice: System media includes digital and non-digital media. Digital media includes flash drives, diskettes, magnetic tapes, external or removable hard disk drives (e.g., solid state, magnetic), compact discs, and digital versatile discs. Non-digital media includes paper and microfilm.
blocks.example: Backup tapes are stored in a locked cabinet accessible only to the backup team.

blocks.text: Control statement
Restrict access to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined types of digital and/or non-digital media] to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined personnel or roles].
**Related controls:** AC-19, AU-9, CP-2, CP-9, CP-10, MA-5, MP-4, MP-6, PE-2, PE-3, SC-12, SC-13, SC-34, SI-12.
**Media Marking.** Mark media with distribution limitations, handling caveats and security markings.
blocks.practice: Security marking refers to the application or use of human-readable security attributes. Digital media includes diskettes, magnetic tapes, external or removable hard disk drives (e.g., solid state, magnetic), flash drives, compact discs, and digital versatile discs. Non-digital media includes paper and microfilm.
blocks.example: Removable drives holding confidential data carry labels showing classification and owner.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Mark system media indicating the distribution limitations, handling caveats, and applicable security markings (if any) of the information; and
**b.** Exempt [Assignment: organization-defined types of media exempted from marking] from marking if the media remain within [Assignment: organization-defined controlled areas].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-16, CP-9, MP-5, PE-22, SI-12.
**Media Storage.** Physically control and securely store media until destroyed or sanitised.
blocks.practice: System media includes digital and non-digital media. Digital media includes flash drives, diskettes, magnetic tapes, external or removable hard disk drives (e.g., solid state, magnetic), compact discs, and digital versatile discs. Non-digital media includes paper and microfilm.
blocks.example: Archived paper records are kept in a secure records room with access logging.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Physically control and securely store [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined types of digital and/or non-digital media] within [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined controlled areas] ; and
**b.** Protect system media types defined in MP-4a until the media are destroyed or sanitized using approved equipment, techniques, and procedures.

**Media Transport.** Protect and control media during transport outside controlled areas, with accountability.
blocks.practice: System media includes digital and non-digital media. Digital media includes flash drives, diskettes, magnetic tapes, external or removable hard disk drives (e.g., solid state and magnetic), compact discs, and digital versatile discs. Non-digital media includes microfilm and paper.
blocks.example: Backup drives shipped off-site are encrypted and carried by a bonded courier with chain-of-custody records.

items: **a.** Protect and control [Assignment: organization-defined types of system media] during transport outside of controlled areas using [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined controls];

blocks.practice: Media sanitization applies to all digital and non-digital system media subject to disposal or reuse, whether or not the media is considered removable. Examples include digital media in scanners, copiers, printers, notebook computers, workstations, network components, mobile devices, and non-digital media (e.g., paper and microfilm).
blocks.example: Retired disks are purged or shredded per SP 800-88 and certificates of destruction retained.

items: **a.** Sanitize [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined system media] prior to disposal, release out of organizational control, or release for reuse using [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined sanitization techniques and procedures] ; and

blocks.practice: System media includes both digital and non-digital media. Digital media includes diskettes, magnetic tapes, flash drives, compact discs, digital versatile discs, and removable hard disk drives. Non-digital media includes paper and microfilm. Media use protections also apply to mobile devices with information storage capabilities.
blocks.example: USB storage is blocked on all workstations except approved encrypted drives.

blocks.text: Physical and Environmental Protection protects facilities, equipment and people: physical access, monitoring, visitors, power, fire, water, environmental controls and alternate work sites.

blocks.title: Cloud changes scope
blocks.text: For systems in the cloud, most PE controls are inherited from the provider. You still own PE for your offices, user devices and any on-premises equipment.

items: **PE-7** Visitor Control: incorporated into PE-2, PE-3

blocks.text: **Policy and Procedures.** Maintain a physical and environmental protection policy and procedures, owned and reviewed on schedule.
blocks.practice: Physical and environmental protection policy and procedures address the controls in the PE family that are implemented within systems and organizations. The risk management strategy is an important factor in establishing such policies and procedures. Policies and procedures contribute to security and privacy assurance.
blocks.example: Facilities and security jointly own the physical security policy.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop, document, and disseminate to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined personnel or roles]:
**a.1.** [Selection (one or more): organization-level; mission/business process-level; system-level] physical and environmental protection policy that:
**a.1.(a).** Addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; and
**a.1.(b).** Is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; and
**a.2.** Procedures to facilitate the implementation of the physical and environmental protection policy and the associated physical and environmental protection controls;
**b.** Designate an [Assignment: organization-defined official] to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the physical and environmental protection policy and procedures; and
**c.** Review and update the current physical and environmental protection:
**c.1.** Policy [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events] ; and
**c.2.** Procedures [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AT-3, PM-9, PS-8, SI-12.
**Physical Access Authorizations.** Develop, approve and maintain a list of individuals with authorised physical access, and issue credentials.
blocks.practice: Physical access authorizations apply to employees and visitors. Individuals with permanent physical access authorization credentials are not considered visitors. Authorization credentials include ID badges, identification cards, and smart cards.
blocks.example: Data centre access lists are reviewed monthly and badges disabled for anyone no longer needing access.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop, approve, and maintain a list of individuals with authorized access to the facility where the system resides;
**b.** Issue authorization credentials for facility access;
**c.** Review the access list detailing authorized facility access by individuals [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] ; and
**d.** Remove individuals from the facility access list when access is no longer required.

blocks.text: Enhancements (3 active)
**Related controls:** AT-3, AU-9, IA-4, MA-5, MP-2, PE-3, PE-4, PE-5, PE-8, PM-12, PS-3, PS-4, PS-5, PS-6.
**Physical Access Control.** Enforce physical access authorisations at entry and exit points, and control access to areas within facilities.
blocks.practice: Physical access control applies to employees and visitors. Individuals with permanent physical access authorizations are not considered visitors. Physical access controls for publicly accessible areas may include physical access control logs/records, guards, or physical access devices and barriers to prevent movement from publicly accessible areas to non-public areas.
blocks.example: Badge readers and mantraps control entry to the server room; visitors are escorted.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Enforce physical access authorizations at [Assignment: organization-defined entry and exit points] by:
**a.1.** Verifying individual access authorizations before granting access to the facility; and
**a.2.** Controlling ingress and egress to the facility using [Selection (one or more): [Assignment: organization-defined systems or devices] ; guards];
**b.** Maintain physical access audit logs for [Assignment: organization-defined entry or exit points];
**c.** Control access to areas within the facility designated as publicly accessible by implementing the following controls: [Assignment: organization-defined physical access controls];
**d.** Escort visitors and control visitor activity [Assignment: organization-defined circumstances];
**e.** Secure keys, combinations, and other physical access devices;
**f.** Inventory [Assignment: organization-defined physical access devices] every [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] ; and

**g.** Change combinations and keys [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined frequency] and/or when keys are lost, combinations are compromised, or when individuals possessing the keys or combinations are transferred or terminated.

blocks.text: Enhancements (7 active, 1 withdrawn)
**Related controls:** AT-3, AU-2, AU-6, AU-9, AU-13, CP-10, IA-3, IA-8, MA-5, MP-2, MP-4, PE-2, PE-4, PE-5, PE-8, PS-2 and 7 more.
**Access Control for Transmission.** Control physical access to system distribution and transmission lines.
blocks.practice: Security controls applied to system distribution and transmission lines prevent accidental damage, disruption, and physical tampering. Such controls may also be necessary to prevent eavesdropping or modification of unencrypted transmissions.
blocks.example: Network cabling in shared buildings runs in locked conduits and wiring closets.

blocks.text: Control statement
Control physical access to [Assignment: organization-defined system distribution and transmission lines] within organizational facilities using [Assignment: organization-defined security controls].
**Related controls:** AT-3, IA-4, MP-2, MP-4, PE-2, PE-3, PE-5, PE-9, SC-7, SC-8.

sections.title: PE-5 Access Control for Output Devices

blocks.text: **Access Control for Output Devices.** Control physical access to output devices to prevent unauthorised individuals obtaining output.
blocks.practice: Controlling physical access to output devices includes placing output devices in locked rooms or other secured areas with keypad or card reader access controls and allowing access to authorized individuals only, placing output devices in locations that can be monitored by personnel, installing monitor or screen filters, and using headphones.
blocks.example: Printers in HR use secure release so documents print only when the user badges in.

blocks.text: Control statement
Control physical access to output from [Assignment: organization-defined output devices] to prevent unauthorized individuals from obtaining the output.
Enhancements (1 active, 2 withdrawn)
**Related controls:** PE-2, PE-3, PE-4, PE-18.
**Monitoring Physical Access.** Monitor physical access to detect and respond to incidents, and review access logs.
blocks.practice: Physical access monitoring includes publicly accessible areas within organizational facilities. Examples of physical access monitoring include the employment of guards, video surveillance equipment (i.e., cameras), and sensor devices. Reviewing physical access logs can help identify suspicious activity, anomalous events, or potential threats.
blocks.example: CCTV and badge logs are reviewed after any alarm and sampled monthly.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Monitor physical access to the facility where the system resides to detect and respond to physical security incidents;
**b.** Review physical access logs [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and upon occurrence of [Assignment: organization-defined events] ; and
**c.** Coordinate results of reviews and investigations with the organizational incident response capability.

blocks.text: Enhancements (4 active)
**Related controls:** AU-2, AU-6, AU-9, AU-12, CA-7, CP-10, IR-4, IR-8.
**Visitor Access Records.** Maintain and review visitor access records.
blocks.practice: Visitor access records include the names and organizations of individuals visiting, visitor signatures, forms of identification, dates of access, entry and departure times, purpose of visits, and the names and organizations of individuals visited. Access record reviews determine if access authorizations are current and are still required to support organizational mission and business functions.
blocks.example: Visitor logs record name, organisation, host and times, and are kept for one year.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Maintain visitor access records to the facility where the system resides for [Assignment: organization-defined time period];
**b.** Review visitor access records [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] ; and
**c.** Report anomalies in visitor access records to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel].

blocks.text: Enhancements (2 active, 1 withdrawn)
**Related controls:** PE-2, PE-3, PE-6.
**Power Equipment and Cabling.** Protect power equipment and cabling from damage and destruction.
blocks.practice: Organizations determine the types of protection necessary for the power equipment and cabling employed at different locations that are both internal and external to organizational facilities and environments of operation.
blocks.example: Power distribution units in the data centre are in a restricted area with protected cabling.

blocks.text: Control statement
Protect power equipment and power cabling for the system from damage and destruction.
Enhancements (2 active)
**Related controls:** PE-4.
**Emergency Shutoff.** Provide the ability to shut off power to systems in emergencies, with protected emergency switches.
blocks.practice: Emergency power shutoff primarily applies to organizational facilities that contain concentrations of system resources, including data centers, mainframe computer rooms, server rooms, and areas with computer-controlled machinery.
blocks.example: Emergency power-off buttons near data centre exits are covered to prevent accidental activation.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Provide the capability of shutting off power to [Assignment: organization-defined system or individual system components] in emergency situations;
**b.** Place emergency shutoff switches or devices in [Assignment: organization-defined location] to facilitate access for authorized personnel; and
**c.** Protect emergency power shutoff capability from unauthorized activation.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PE-15.
**Emergency Power.** Provide an uninterruptible power supply for orderly shutdown or transition to long-term alternate power.
blocks.practice: An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) is an electrical system or mechanism that provides emergency power when there is a failure of the main power source. A UPS is typically used to protect computers, data centers, telecommunication equipment, or other electrical equipment where an unexpected power disruption could cause injuries, fatalities, serious mission or business disruption, or loss of data or information.
blocks.example: UPS units keep servers running until the generator starts.

blocks.text: Control statement

Provide an uninterruptible power supply to facilitate [Selection: an orderly shutdown of the system; transition of the system to long-term alternate power] in the event of a primary power source loss.
Enhancements (2 active)

rows: **PE-11(1)** Alternate Power Supply — Minimal Operational Capability

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AT-3, CP-2, CP-7.
**Emergency Lighting.** Provide automatic emergency lighting that covers exits and evacuation routes.
blocks.practice: The provision of emergency lighting applies primarily to organizational facilities that contain concentrations of system resources, including data centers, server rooms, and mainframe computer rooms. Emergency lighting provisions for the system are described in the contingency plan for the organization.
blocks.example: Emergency lights activate automatically during power loss in the operations centre.

blocks.text: Control statement
Employ and maintain automatic emergency lighting for the system that activates in the event of a power outage or disruption and that covers emergency exits and evacuation routes within the facility.
Enhancements (1 active)
**Related controls:** CP-2, CP-7.
**Fire Protection.** Employ fire detection and suppression systems supported by an independent energy source.
blocks.practice: The provision of fire detection and suppression systems applies primarily to organizational facilities that contain concentrations of system resources, including data centers, server rooms, and mainframe computer rooms. Fire detection and suppression systems that may require an independent energy source include sprinkler systems and smoke detectors.
blocks.example: The data centre uses early smoke detection and a gas-based suppression system.

blocks.text: Control statement
Employ and maintain fire detection and suppression systems that are supported by an independent energy source.
Enhancements (3 active, 1 withdrawn)

rows: **PE-13(1)** Detection Systems — Automatic Activation and Notification
**PE-13(2)** Suppression Systems — Automatic Activation and Notification

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AT-3.
**Environmental Controls.** Maintain and monitor environmental controls such as temperature and humidity.
blocks.practice: The provision of environmental controls applies primarily to organizational facilities that contain concentrations of system resources (e.g., data centers, mainframe computer rooms, and server rooms).
blocks.example: Sensors alert facilities when server room temperature exceeds 27°C.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Maintain [Selection (one or more): temperature; humidity; pressure; radiation; [Assignment: organization-defined environmental control] ] levels within the facility where the system resides at [Assignment: organization-defined acceptable levels] ; and
**b.** Monitor environmental control levels [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].

blocks.text: Enhancements (2 active)
**Related controls:** AT-3, CP-2.
**Water Damage Protection.** Protect systems from water damage with accessible, working master shutoff valves.
blocks.practice: The provision of water damage protection primarily applies to organizational facilities that contain concentrations of system resources, including data centers, server rooms, and mainframe computer rooms. Isolation valves can be employed in addition to or in lieu of master shutoff valves to shut off water supplies in specific areas of concern without affecting entire organizations.
blocks.example: Water leak detectors under raised floors trigger alarms and staff know where shutoff valves are.

blocks.text: Control statement
Protect the system from damage resulting from water leakage by providing master shutoff or isolation valves that are accessible, working properly, and known to key personnel.
Enhancements (1 active)
**Related controls:** AT-3, PE-10.
**Delivery and Removal.** Authorise and control delivery and removal of system components, and keep records.
blocks.practice: Enforcing authorizations for entry and exit of system components may require restricting access to delivery areas and isolating the areas from the system and media libraries.
blocks.example: Equipment leaving the data centre requires a signed removal form checked by security.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Authorize and control [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined types of system components] entering and exiting the facility; and
**b.** Maintain records of the system components.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** CM-3, CM-8, MA-2, MA-3, MP-5, PE-20, SR-2, SR-3, SR-4, SR-6.
**Alternate Work Site.** Define controls for alternate work sites (e.g. home), assess them and provide a way to communicate with security staff.
blocks.practice: Alternate work sites include government facilities or the private residences of employees. While distinct from alternative processing sites, alternate work sites can provide readily available alternate locations during contingency operations. Organizations can define different sets of controls for specific alternate work sites or types of sites depending on the work-related activities conducted at the sites.
blocks.example: Home workers follow a remote work standard covering screen privacy, secure Wi-Fi and reporting.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Determine and document the [Assignment: organization-defined alternate work sites] allowed for use by employees;
**b.** Employ the following controls at alternate work sites: [Assignment: organization-defined controls];
**c.** Assess the effectiveness of controls at alternate work sites; and
**d.** Provide a means for employees to communicate with information security and privacy personnel in case of incidents.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-17, AC-18, CP-7.
**Location of System Components.** Position system components to minimise damage from physical and environmental hazards and unauthorised access.
blocks.practice: Physical and environmental hazards include floods, fires, tornadoes, earthquakes, hurricanes, terrorism, vandalism, an electromagnetic pulse, electrical interference, and other forms of incoming electromagnetic radiation. Organizations consider the location of entry points where unauthorized individuals, while not being granted access, might nonetheless be near systems.
blocks.example: Servers are placed away from windows, water pipes and public areas.

blocks.text: Control statement

Position system components within the facility to minimize potential damage from [Assignment: organization-defined physical and environmental hazards] and to minimize the opportunity for unauthorized access.
**Related controls:** CP-2, PE-5, PE-19, PE-20, RA-3.
**Information Leakage.** Protect the system from information leakage due to electromagnetic signal emanations.
blocks.practice: Information leakage is the intentional or unintentional release of data or information to an untrusted environment from electromagnetic signals emanations.
blocks.example: Rooms processing highly classified data meet TEMPEST emanation standards.

blocks.text: Control statement
Protect the system from information leakage due to electromagnetic signals emanations.
Enhancements (1 active)
**Related controls:** AC-18, PE-18, PE-20.
**Asset Monitoring and Tracking.** Monitor and track the location and movement of defined assets within controlled areas.
blocks.practice: Asset location technologies can help ensure that critical assets—including vehicles, equipment, and system components—remain in authorized locations. Organizations consult with the Office of the General Counsel and senior agency official for privacy regarding the deployment and use of asset location technologies to address potential privacy concerns.
blocks.example: RFID tags track high-value equipment movement in the data centre.

blocks.text: Control statement

Employ [Assignment: organization-defined asset location technologies] to track and monitor the location and movement of [Assignment: organization-defined assets] within [Assignment: organization-defined controlled areas].
**Related controls:** CM-8, PE-16, PM-8.
**Electromagnetic Pulse Protection.** Protect system components against electromagnetic pulse damage.
blocks.practice: An electromagnetic pulse (EMP) is a short burst of electromagnetic energy that is spread over a range of frequencies. Such energy bursts may be natural or man-made. EMP interference may be disruptive or damaging to electronic equipment. Protective measures used to mitigate EMP risk include shielding, surge suppressors, ferro-resonant transformers, and earth grounding.
blocks.example: Critical infrastructure control rooms use EMP-hardened enclosures.

blocks.text: Control statement
Employ [Assignment: organization-defined protective measures] against electromagnetic pulse damage for [Assignment: organization-defined system and system components].
**Related controls:** PE-18, PE-19.
**Component Marking.** Mark system hardware components to indicate the impact level or classification of information they may process.
blocks.practice: Hardware components that may require marking include input and output devices. Input devices include desktop and notebook computers, keyboards, tablets, and smart phones. Output devices include printers, monitors/video displays, facsimile machines, scanners, copiers, and audio devices. Permissions controlling output to the output devices are addressed in [AC-3](#ac-3) or [AC-4](#ac-4) .
blocks.example: Workstations approved for secret processing carry colour-coded labels.

blocks.text: Control statement

Mark [Assignment: organization-defined system hardware components] indicating the impact level or classification level of the information permitted to be processed, stored, or transmitted by the hardware component.
**Related controls:** AC-3, AC-4, AC-16, MP-3.
**Facility Location.** Plan the location of facilities considering physical and environmental hazards, and consider site risk in risk strategy.
blocks.practice: Physical and environmental hazards include floods, fires, tornadoes, earthquakes, hurricanes, terrorism, vandalism, an electromagnetic pulse, electrical interference, and other forms of incoming electromagnetic radiation. The location of system components within the facility is addressed in [PE-18](#pe-18).
blocks.example: A new data centre site is selected outside flood zones and away from flight paths.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Plan the location or site of the facility where the system resides considering physical and environmental hazards; and
**b.** For existing facilities, consider the physical and environmental hazards in the organizational risk management strategy.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** CP-2, PE-18, PE-19, PM-8, PM-9, RA-3.

blocks.title: The SSP is the centre
blocks.text: PL-2 requires the system security and privacy plans that describe the system, its boundary and how each control is implemented. Assessors start here.
Withdrawn controls

blocks.text: **Policy and Procedures.** Maintain a planning policy and procedures, owned and reviewed on schedule.
blocks.practice: Planning policy and procedures for the controls in the PL family implemented within systems and organizations. The risk management strategy is an important factor in establishing such policies and procedures. Policies and procedures contribute to security and privacy assurance. Therefore, it is important that security and privacy programs collaborate on their development.
blocks.example: The GRC office maintains the planning policy that defines SSP content and review cycles.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop, document, and disseminate to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined personnel or roles]:
**a.1.** [Selection (one or more): organization-level; mission/business process-level; system-level] planning policy that:
**a.1.(a).** Addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; and
**a.1.(b).** Is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; and
**a.2.** Procedures to facilitate the implementation of the planning policy and the associated planning controls;
**b.** Designate an [Assignment: organization-defined official] to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the planning policy and procedures; and
**c.** Review and update the current planning:
**c.1.** Policy [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events] ; and
**c.2.** Procedures [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PM-9, PS-8, SI-12.

sections.title: PL-2 System Security and Privacy Plans

blocks.text: **System Security and Privacy Plans.** Develop and maintain system security and privacy plans that describe the system, its boundary, environment, and how controls are implemented.
blocks.practice: System security and privacy plans are scoped to the system and system components within the defined authorization boundary and contain an overview of the security and privacy requirements for the system and the controls selected to satisfy the requirements.
blocks.example: Each system has an SSP with its categorisation, boundary diagram and control implementation statements, updated after major changes.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop security and privacy plans for the system that:
**a.1.** Are consistent with the organization’s enterprise architecture;
**a.2.** Explicitly define the constituent system components;
**a.3.** Describe the operational context of the system in terms of mission and business processes;
**a.4.** Identify the individuals that fulfill system roles and responsibilities;
**a.5.** Identify the information types processed, stored, and transmitted by the system;
**a.6.** Provide the security categorization of the system, including supporting rationale;
**a.7.** Describe any specific threats to the system that are of concern to the organization;
**a.8.** Provide the results of a privacy risk assessment for systems processing personally identifiable information;
**a.9.** Describe the operational environment for the system and any dependencies on or connections to other systems or system components;
**a.10.** Provide an overview of the security and privacy requirements for the system;
**a.11.** Identify any relevant control baselines or overlays, if applicable;
**a.12.** Describe the controls in place or planned for meeting the security and privacy requirements, including a rationale for any tailoring decisions;
**a.13.** Include risk determinations for security and privacy architecture and design decisions;
**a.14.** Include security- and privacy-related activities affecting the system that require planning and coordination with [Assignment: organization-defined individuals or groups] ; and
**a.15.** Are reviewed and approved by the authorizing official or designated representative prior to plan implementation.
**b.** Distribute copies of the plans and communicate subsequent changes to the plans to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles];
**c.** Review the plans [Assignment: organization-defined frequency];
**d.** Update the plans to address changes to the system and environment of operation or problems identified during plan implementation or control assessments; and
**e.** Protect the plans from unauthorized disclosure and modification.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-2, AC-6, AC-14, AC-17, AC-20, CA-2, CA-3, CA-7, CM-9, CM-13, CP-2, CP-4, IR-4, IR-8, MA-4, MA-5 and 21 more.
**Rules of Behavior.** Establish rules of behaviour for users and obtain their signed acknowledgement.
blocks.practice: Rules of behavior represent a type of access agreement for organizational users. Other types of access agreements include nondisclosure agreements, conflict-of-interest agreements, and acceptable use agreements (see [PS-6](#ps-6) ).
blocks.example: Users accept the acceptable use rules at onboarding and yearly in the learning platform.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Establish and provide to individuals requiring access to the system, the rules that describe their responsibilities and expected behavior for information and system usage, security, and privacy;

**b.** Receive a documented acknowledgment from such individuals, indicating that they have read, understand, and agree to abide by the rules of behavior, before authorizing access to information and the system;
**c.** Review and update the rules of behavior [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] ; and

**d.** Require individuals who have acknowledged a previous version of the rules of behavior to read and re-acknowledge [Selection (one or more): [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] ; when the rules are revised or updated].

rows: **PL-4(1)** Social Media and External Site/Application Usage Restrictions

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-2, AC-6, AC-8, AC-9, AC-17, AC-18, AC-19, AC-20, AT-2, AT-3, CM-11, IA-2, IA-4, IA-5, MP-7, PS-6 and 3 more.
**Concept of Operations.** Develop a concept of operations (CONOPS) describing how the organisation intends to operate the system from a security and privacy view.
blocks.practice: The CONOPS may be included in the security or privacy plans for the system or in other system development life cycle documents. The CONOPS is a living document that requires updating throughout the system development life cycle.
blocks.example: The CONOPS for a new drone programme explains how data is collected, transmitted and protected.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop a Concept of Operations (CONOPS) for the system describing how the organization intends to operate the system from the perspective of information security and privacy; and
**b.** Review and update the CONOPS [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PL-2, SA-2, SI-12.
**Security and Privacy Architectures.** Develop security and privacy architectures describing requirements, approach and relationship to the enterprise architecture.
blocks.practice: The security and privacy architectures at the system level are consistent with the organization-wide security and privacy architectures described in [PM-7](#pm-7) , which are integral to and developed as part of the enterprise architecture.
blocks.example: The security architecture defines zones, identity integration and encryption approach for the new cloud platform.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop security and privacy architectures for the system that:
**a.1.** Describe the requirements and approach to be taken for protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of organizational information;
**a.2.** Describe the requirements and approach to be taken for processing personally identifiable information to minimize privacy risk to individuals;
**a.3.** Describe how the architectures are integrated into and support the enterprise architecture; and
**a.4.** Describe any assumptions about, and dependencies on, external systems and services;
**b.** Review and update the architectures [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] to reflect changes in the enterprise architecture; and
**c.** Reflect planned architecture changes in security and privacy plans, Concept of Operations (CONOPS), criticality analysis, organizational procedures, and procurements and acquisitions.

blocks.text: Enhancements (2 active)
**Related controls:** CM-2, CM-6, PL-2, PL-7, PL-9, PM-5, PM-7, RA-9, SA-3, SA-5, SA-8, SA-17, SC-7.
**Central Management.** Centrally manage defined controls and related processes.
blocks.practice: Central management refers to organization-wide management and implementation of selected controls and processes. This includes planning, implementing, assessing, authorizing, and monitoring the organization-defined, centrally managed controls and processes.
blocks.example: Endpoint security settings and privacy notices are managed centrally rather than per system.

blocks.text: Control statement
Centrally manage [Assignment: organization-defined controls and related processes].
**Related controls:** PL-8, PM-9.
**Baseline Selection.** Select a control baseline for the system.
blocks.practice: Control baselines are predefined sets of controls specifically assembled to address the protection needs of a group, organization, or community of interest. Controls are chosen for baselines to either satisfy mandates imposed by laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines or address threats common to all users of the baseline under the assumptions specific to the baseline.
blocks.example: Based on its moderate categorisation, the HR system starts from the SP 800-53B moderate baseline.

blocks.text: Control statement
Select a control baseline for the system.
**Related controls:** PL-2, PL-11, RA-2, RA-3, SA-8.
**Baseline Tailoring.** Tailor the selected control baseline by applying tailoring actions.
blocks.practice: The concept of tailoring allows organizations to specialize or customize a set of baseline controls by applying a defined set of tailoring actions.
blocks.example: The team tailors the baseline, marking physical controls as inherited from the cloud provider and adding privacy controls.

blocks.text: Control statement
Tailor the selected control baseline by applying specified tailoring actions.
**Related controls:** PL-10, RA-2, RA-3, RA-9, SA-8.

blocks.text: Program Management covers organisation-wide security and privacy programme controls: programme plans, leadership roles, resources, inventories, risk strategy, enterprise architecture, workforce, supply chain strategy and continuous monitoring strategy.

blocks.title: Not in the security baselines
blocks.text: PM controls are implemented at the organisation level, independent of any system's impact level, so SP 800-53B does not allocate them to the Low, Moderate or High baselines. Some appear in the privacy baseline.
**Information Security Program Plan.** Develop and disseminate an organisation-wide information security programme plan describing the programme, roles and controls.
blocks.practice: An information security program plan is a formal document that provides an overview of the security requirements for an organization-wide information security program and describes the program management controls and common controls in place or planned for meeting those requirements. An information security program plan can be represented in a single document or compilations of documents.
blocks.example: The group information security programme plan describes governance, common controls and responsibilities across subsidiaries.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop and disseminate an organization-wide information security program plan that:

**a.1.** Provides an overview of the requirements for the security program and a description of the security program management controls and common controls in place or planned for meeting those requirements;
**a.2.** Includes the identification and assignment of roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance;
**a.3.** Reflects the coordination among organizational entities responsible for information security; and

**a.4.** Is approved by a senior official with responsibility and accountability for the risk being incurred to organizational operations (including mission, functions, image, and reputation), organizational assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation;
**b.** Review and update the organization-wide information security program plan [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events] ; and
**c.** Protect the information security program plan from unauthorized disclosure and modification.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PL-2, PM-18, PM-30, RA-9, SI-12, SR-2.

sections.title: PM-2 Information Security Program Leadership Role

blocks.text: **Information Security Program Leadership Role.** Appoint a senior agency information security officer (or equivalent) with the mission and resources to run the programme.
blocks.practice: The senior agency information security officer is an organizational official. For federal agencies (as defined by applicable laws, executive orders, regulations, directives, policies, and standards), this official is the senior agency information security officer. Organizations may also refer to this official as the senior information security officer or chief information security officer.
blocks.example: The board appoints a CISO reporting to the CEO with authority over the security programme.

blocks.text: Control statement
Appoint a senior agency information security officer with the mission and resources to coordinate, develop, implement, and maintain an organization-wide information security program.

sections.title: PM-3 Information Security and Privacy Resources

blocks.text: **Information Security and Privacy Resources.** Include resources for the security and privacy programmes in capital planning and investment requests.
blocks.practice: Organizations consider establishing champions for information security and privacy and, as part of including the necessary resources, assign specialized expertise and resources as needed. Organizations may designate and empower an Investment Review Board or similar group to manage and provide oversight for the information security and privacy aspects of the capital planning and investment control process.
blocks.example: Every IT investment proposal includes a line for security and privacy costs.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Include the resources needed to implement the information security and privacy programs in capital planning and investment requests and document all exceptions to this requirement;

**b.** Prepare documentation required for addressing information security and privacy programs in capital planning and investment requests in accordance with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards; and
**c.** Make available for expenditure, the planned information security and privacy resources.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PM-4, SA-2.

sections.title: PM-4 Plan of Action and Milestones Process

blocks.text: **Plan of Action and Milestones Process.** Implement a process to maintain POA&Ms for the programme and systems, consistent with reporting requirements.
blocks.practice: The plan of action and milestones is a key organizational document and is subject to reporting requirements established by the Office of Management and Budget. Organizations develop plans of action and milestones with an organization-wide perspective, prioritizing risk response actions and ensuring consistency with the goals and objectives of the organization.
blocks.example: A central GRC tool aggregates POA&Ms from all systems for enterprise reporting.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Implement a process to ensure that plans of action and milestones for the information security, privacy, and supply chain risk management programs and associated organizational systems:
**a.1.** Are developed and maintained;

**a.2.** Document the remedial information security, privacy, and supply chain risk management actions to adequately respond to risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation; and
**a.3.** Are reported in accordance with established reporting requirements.
**b.** Review plans of action and milestones for consistency with the organizational risk management strategy and organization-wide priorities for risk response actions.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** CA-5, CA-7, PM-3, RA-7, SI-12.
**System Inventory.** Develop and update an inventory of organisational systems.
blocks.practice: [OMB A-130](#27847491-5ce1-4f6a-a1e4-9e483782f0ef) provides guidance on developing systems inventories and associated reporting requirements. System inventory refers to an organization-wide inventory of systems, not system components as described in [CM-8](#cm-8).
blocks.example: The enterprise system inventory lists every system, owner, categorisation and authorisation status.

blocks.text: Control statement
Develop and update [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] an inventory of organizational systems.
Enhancements (1 active)
**Measures of Performance.** Develop, monitor and report on security and privacy measures of performance.
blocks.practice: Measures of performance are outcome-based metrics used by an organization to measure the effectiveness or efficiency of the information security and privacy programs and the controls employed in support of the program. To facilitate security and privacy risk management, organizations consider aligning measures of performance with the organizational risk tolerance as defined in the risk management strategy.
blocks.example: Quarterly metrics track MFA coverage, patch timeliness and privacy request handling.

blocks.text: Control statement
Develop, monitor, and report on the results of information security and privacy measures of performance.
**Related controls:** CA-7, PM-9.
**Enterprise Architecture.** Develop and maintain an enterprise architecture that considers security, privacy and risk.
blocks.practice: The integration of security and privacy requirements and controls into the enterprise architecture helps to ensure that security and privacy considerations are addressed throughout the system development life cycle and are explicitly related to the organization’s mission and business processes.
blocks.example: Security and privacy principles are part of the enterprise architecture and reviewed by the architecture board.

blocks.text: Control statement

Develop and maintain an enterprise architecture with consideration for information security, privacy, and the resulting risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation.
Enhancements (1 active)
**Related controls:** AU-6, PL-2, PL-8, PM-11, RA-2, SA-3, SA-8, SA-17.
**Critical Infrastructure Plan.** Address security and privacy in critical infrastructure and key resources protection plans.
blocks.practice: Protection strategies are based on the prioritization of critical assets and resources. The requirement and guidance for defining critical infrastructure and key resources and for preparing an associated critical infrastructure protection plan are found in applicable laws, executive orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidelines.
blocks.example: A utility's critical infrastructure plan includes cyber protection of substations.

blocks.text: Control statement
Address information security and privacy issues in the development, documentation, and updating of a critical infrastructure and key resources protection plan.
**Related controls:** CP-2, CP-4, PE-18, PL-2, PM-9, PM-11, PM-18, RA-3, SI-12.
**Risk Management Strategy.** Develop a comprehensive risk management strategy, including risk tolerance, and implement it consistently.
blocks.practice: An organization-wide risk management strategy includes an expression of the security and privacy risk tolerance for the organization, security and privacy risk mitigation strategies, acceptable risk assessment methodologies, a process for evaluating security and privacy risk across the organization with respect to the organization’s risk tolerance, and approaches for monitoring risk over time.
blocks.example: The board-approved risk strategy defines cyber risk appetite and escalation thresholds.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develops a comprehensive strategy to manage:
**a.1.** Security risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation associated with the operation and use of organizational systems; and
**a.2.** Privacy risk to individuals resulting from the authorized processing of personally identifiable information;
**b.** Implement the risk management strategy consistently across the organization; and
**c.** Review and update the risk management strategy [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] or as required, to address organizational changes.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-1, AU-1, AT-1, CA-1, CA-2, CA-5, CA-6, CA-7, CM-1, CP-1, IA-1, IR-1, MA-1, MP-1, PE-1, PL-1 and 21 more.
**Authorization Process.** Manage the security and privacy state of systems through authorisation processes and designate individuals to fulfil roles.
blocks.practice: Authorization processes for organizational systems and environments of operation require the implementation of an organization-wide risk management process and associated security and privacy standards and guidelines. Specific roles for risk management processes include a risk executive (function) and designated authorizing officials for each organizational system and common control provider.
blocks.example: The organisation defines authorising officials for each business area.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Manage the security and privacy state of organizational systems and the environments in which those systems operate through authorization processes;
**b.** Designate individuals to fulfill specific roles and responsibilities within the organizational risk management process; and
**c.** Integrate the authorization processes into an organization-wide risk management program.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** CA-6, CA-7, PL-2.

sections.title: PM-11 Mission and Business Process Definition

blocks.text: **Mission and Business Process Definition.** Define mission and business processes with security and privacy in mind, and determine protection needs.
blocks.practice: Protection needs are technology-independent capabilities that are required to counter threats to organizations, individuals, systems, and the Nation through the compromise of information (i.e., loss of confidentiality, integrity, availability, or privacy).
blocks.example: Process definitions for claims handling include protection needs for the data they use.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Define organizational mission and business processes with consideration for information security and privacy and the resulting risk to organizational operations, organizational assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation; and
**b.** Determine information protection and personally identifiable information processing needs arising from the defined mission and business processes; and
**c.** Review and revise the mission and business processes [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** CP-2, PL-2, PM-7, PM-8, RA-2, RA-3, RA-9, SA-2.
**Insider Threat Program.** Implement an insider threat programme with a cross-discipline incident handling team.
blocks.practice: Organizations that handle classified information are required, under Executive Order 13587 [EO 13587](#0af071a6-cf8e-48ee-8c82-fe91efa20f94) and the National Insider Threat Policy [ODNI NITP](#06d74ea9-2178-449c-a9c5-b2980f804ac8) , to establish insider threat programs.
blocks.example: HR, legal, security and IT jointly run an insider threat programme with defined triggers.

blocks.text: Control statement
Implement an insider threat program that includes a cross-discipline insider threat incident handling team.
**Related controls:** AC-6, AT-2, AU-6, AU-7, AU-10, AU-12, AU-13, CA-7, IA-4, IR-4, MP-7, PE-2, PM-16, PS-3, PS-4, PS-5 and 6 more.
**Security and Privacy Workforce.** Establish a security and privacy workforce development and improvement programme.
blocks.practice: Security and privacy workforce development and improvement programs include defining the knowledge, skills, and abilities needed to perform security and privacy duties and tasks; developing role-based training programs for individuals assigned security and privacy roles and responsibilities; and providing standards and guidelines for measuring and building individual qualifications for incumbents and applicants for security- and privacy-related positions.
blocks.example: A skills framework defines security roles and funds certifications and career paths.

blocks.text: Control statement
Establish a security and privacy workforce development and improvement program.
**Related controls:** AT-2, AT-3.
**Testing, Training, and Monitoring.** Implement a process to plan, conduct and review security and privacy testing, training and monitoring activities.
blocks.practice: A process for organization-wide security and privacy testing, training, and monitoring helps ensure that organizations provide oversight for testing, training, and monitoring activities and that those activities are coordinated.
blocks.example: An annual calendar coordinates pen tests, exercises and training across the organisation.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Implement a process for ensuring that organizational plans for conducting security and privacy testing, training, and monitoring activities associated with organizational systems:
**a.1.** Are developed and maintained; and
**a.2.** Continue to be executed; and
**b.** Review testing, training, and monitoring plans for consistency with the organizational risk management strategy and organization-wide priorities for risk response actions.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AT-2, AT-3, CA-7, CP-4, IR-3, PM-12, SI-4.

sections.title: PM-15 Security and Privacy Groups and Associations

blocks.text: **Security and Privacy Groups and Associations.** Establish contact with security and privacy groups and associations to share information and stay current.
blocks.practice: Ongoing contact with security and privacy groups and associations is important in an environment of rapidly changing technologies and threats. Groups and associations include special interest groups, professional associations, forums, news groups, users’ groups, and peer groups of security and privacy professionals in similar organizations.
blocks.example: The security team participates in the national CERT community and a financial sector ISAC.

blocks.text: Control statement
Establish and institutionalize contact with selected groups and associations within the security and privacy communities:

items: **a.** To facilitate ongoing security and privacy education and training for organizational personnel;
**b.** To maintain currency with recommended security and privacy practices, techniques, and technologies; and
**c.** To share current security and privacy information, including threats, vulnerabilities, and incidents.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** SA-11, SI-5.
**Threat Awareness Program.** Implement a threat awareness programme including cross-organisation information sharing.
blocks.practice: Because of the constantly changing and increasing sophistication of adversaries, especially the advanced persistent threat (APT), it may be more likely that adversaries can successfully breach or compromise organizational systems.
blocks.example: Threat intelligence is shared with peer banks and fed into the SOC's detection rules.

blocks.text: Control statement
Implement a threat awareness program that includes a cross-organization information-sharing capability for threat intelligence.
Enhancements (1 active)

rows: **PM-16(1)** Automated Means for Sharing Threat Intelligence

blocks.text: **Related controls:** IR-4, PM-12.

sections.title: PM-17 Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information on External Systems

blocks.text: **Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information on External Systems.** Establish policy and procedures to protect controlled unclassified information processed on external systems.
blocks.practice: Controlled unclassified information is defined by the National Archives and Records Administration along with the safeguarding and dissemination requirements for such information and is codified in [32 CFR 2002](#91f992fb-f668-4c91-a50f-0f05b95ccee3) and, specifically for systems external to the federal organization, [32 CFR 2002.14h](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2017-title32-vol6/xml/CFR-2017-title32-vol6-part2002.xml) .
blocks.example: Contractors handling CUI must meet NIST SP 800-171 requirements on their systems.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Establish policy and procedures to ensure that requirements for the protection of controlled unclassified information that is processed, stored or transmitted on external systems, are implemented in accordance with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, policies, regulations, and standards; and
**b.** Review and update the policy and procedures [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined frequency].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** CA-6, PM-10.
**Privacy Program Plan.** Develop and disseminate an organisation-wide privacy programme plan.
blocks.practice: A privacy program plan is a formal document that provides an overview of an organization’s privacy program, including a description of the structure of the privacy program, the resources dedicated to the privacy program, the role of the senior agency official for privacy and other privacy officials and staff, the strategic goals and objectives of the privacy program, and the program management controls and common controls in place or planned for meeting applicable privacy requirements and managing privacy risks.
blocks.example: The privacy programme plan describes the DPO's role, policies and privacy controls.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop and disseminate an organization-wide privacy program plan that provides an overview of the agency’s privacy program, and:
**a.1.** Includes a description of the structure of the privacy program and the resources dedicated to the privacy program;

**a.2.** Provides an overview of the requirements for the privacy program and a description of the privacy program management controls and common controls in place or planned for meeting those requirements;
**a.3.** Includes the role of the senior agency official for privacy and the identification and assignment of roles of other privacy officials and staff and their responsibilities;
**a.4.** Describes management commitment, compliance, and the strategic goals and objectives of the privacy program;
**a.5.** Reflects coordination among organizational entities responsible for the different aspects of privacy; and

**a.6.** Is approved by a senior official with responsibility and accountability for the privacy risk being incurred to organizational operations (including mission, functions, image, and reputation), organizational assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation; and

**b.** Update the plan [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and to address changes in federal privacy laws and policy and organizational changes and problems identified during plan implementation or privacy control assessments.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PM-8, PM-9, PM-19.
**Privacy Program Leadership Role.** Appoint a senior agency official for privacy (or equivalent) with authority over the privacy programme.
blocks.practice: The privacy officer is an organizational official. For federal agencies—as defined by applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines—this official is designated as the senior agency official for privacy. Organizations may also refer to this official as the chief privacy officer.
blocks.example: A Chief Privacy Officer leads privacy across the organisation.

blocks.text: Control statement

Appoint a senior agency official for privacy with the authority, mission, accountability, and resources to coordinate, develop, and implement, applicable privacy requirements and manage privacy risks through the organization-wide privacy program.
**Related controls:** PM-18, PM-20, PM-23, PM-24, PM-27.

sections.title: PM-20 Dissemination of Privacy Program Information

blocks.text: **Dissemination of Privacy Program Information.** Publish information about the privacy programme, such as privacy policies and contact details, on public websites.
blocks.practice: For federal agencies, the webpage is located at www.[agency].gov/privacy.
blocks.example: The public privacy page explains practices and how to contact the privacy office.

blocks.text: Control statement
Maintain a central resource webpage on the organization’s principal public website that serves as a central source of information about the organization’s privacy program and that:

items: **a.** Ensures that the public has access to information about organizational privacy activities and can communicate with its senior agency official for privacy;
**b.** Ensures that organizational privacy practices and reports are publicly available; and
**c.** Employs publicly facing email addresses and/or phone lines to enable the public to provide feedback and/or direct questions to privacy offices regarding privacy practices.

blocks.text: Enhancements (1 active)

rows: **PM-20(1)** Privacy Policies on Websites, Applications, and Digital Services

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-3, PM-19, PT-5, PT-6, PT-7, RA-8.
**Accounting of Disclosures.** Keep an accurate accounting of disclosures of PII, and make it available to individuals on request where required.
blocks.practice: The purpose of accounting of disclosures is to allow individuals to learn to whom their personally identifiable information has been disclosed, to provide a basis for subsequently advising recipients of any corrected or disputed personally identifiable information, and to provide an audit trail for subsequent reviews of organizational compliance with conditions for disclosures.
blocks.example: Disclosures of customer records to authorities are logged with date, recipient and purpose.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop and maintain an accurate accounting of disclosures of personally identifiable information, including:
**a.1.** Date, nature, and purpose of each disclosure; and
**a.2.** Name and address, or other contact information of the individual or organization to which the disclosure was made;
**b.** Retain the accounting of disclosures for the length of the time the personally identifiable information is maintained or five years after the disclosure is made, whichever is longer; and
**c.** Make the accounting of disclosures available to the individual to whom the personally identifiable information relates upon request.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-3, AU-2, PT-2.

sections.title: PM-22 Personally Identifiable Information Quality Management

blocks.text: **Personally Identifiable Information Quality Management.** Develop and document an organisation-wide policy for PII quality management (accuracy, relevance, timeliness, completeness).
blocks.practice: Personally identifiable information quality management includes steps that organizations take to confirm the accuracy and relevance of personally identifiable information throughout the information life cycle. The information life cycle includes the creation, collection, use, processing, storage, maintenance, dissemination, disclosure, and disposition of personally identifiable information.
blocks.example: Customers can correct their data online, and data quality checks run monthly.

blocks.text: Control statement
Develop and document organization-wide policies and procedures for:

items: **a.** Reviewing for the accuracy, relevance, timeliness, and completeness of personally identifiable information across the information life cycle;
**b.** Correcting or deleting inaccurate or outdated personally identifiable information;
**c.** Disseminating notice of corrected or deleted personally identifiable information to individuals or other appropriate entities; and
**d.** Appeals of adverse decisions on correction or deletion requests.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PM-23, SI-18.
**Data Governance Body.** Establish a data governance body with defined roles and responsibilities.
blocks.practice: A Data Governance Body can help ensure that the organization has coherent policies and the ability to balance the utility of data with security and privacy requirements.
blocks.example: A data governance council sets data standards and ownership across business units.

blocks.text: Control statement
Establish a Data Governance Body consisting of [Assignment: organization-defined roles] with [Assignment: organization-defined responsibilities].
**Related controls:** AT-2, AT-3, PM-19, PM-22, PM-24, PT-7, SI-4, SI-19.
**Data Integrity Board.** Establish a data integrity board to oversee computer matching agreements (US federal Privacy Act requirement).
blocks.practice: A Data Integrity Board is the board of senior officials designated by the head of a federal agency and is responsible for, among other things, reviewing the agency’s proposals to conduct or participate in a matching program and conducting an annual review of all matching programs in which the agency has participated.
blocks.example: A federal agency's data integrity board reviews and approves computer matching programmes.

blocks.text: Control statement
Establish a Data Integrity Board to:

items: **a.** Review proposals to conduct or participate in a matching program; and
**b.** Conduct an annual review of all matching programs in which the agency has participated.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-4, PM-19, PM-23, PT-2, PT-8.

sections.title: PM-25 Minimization of Personally Identifiable Information Used in Testing, Training, and Research

blocks.text: **Minimization of Personally Identifiable Information Used in Testing, Training, and Research.** Minimise the use of PII in testing, training and research, and approve its use where necessary.
blocks.practice: The use of personally identifiable information in testing, research, and training increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse of such information. Organizations consult with the senior agency official for privacy and/or legal counsel to ensure that the use of personally identifiable information in testing, training, and research is compatible with the original purpose for which it was collected.
blocks.example: Test environments use synthetic or masked data unless the privacy office approves otherwise.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop, document, and implement policies and procedures that address the use of personally identifiable information for internal testing, training, and research;
**b.** Limit or minimize the amount of personally identifiable information used for internal testing, training, and research purposes;
**c.** Authorize the use of personally identifiable information when such information is required for internal testing, training, and research; and
**d.** Review and update policies and procedures [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined frequency].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PM-23, PT-3, SA-3, SA-8, SI-12.
**Complaint Management.** Implement a process to receive and respond to privacy complaints, concerns or questions.
blocks.practice: Complaints, concerns, and questions from individuals can serve as valuable sources of input to organizations and ultimately improve operational models, uses of technology, data collection practices, and controls. Mechanisms that can be used by the public include telephone hotline, email, or web-based forms.
blocks.example: Privacy complaints are logged, acknowledged within five days and resolved with tracked outcomes.

blocks.text: Control statement
Implement a process for receiving and responding to complaints, concerns, or questions from individuals about the organizational security and privacy practices that includes:

items: **a.** Mechanisms that are easy to use and readily accessible by the public;
**b.** All information necessary for successfully filing complaints;
**c.** Tracking mechanisms to ensure all complaints received are reviewed and addressed within [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined time period];
**d.** Acknowledgement of receipt of complaints, concerns, or questions from individuals within [Assignment: organization-defined time period] ; and
**e.** Response to complaints, concerns, or questions from individuals within [Assignment: organization-defined time period].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** IR-7, IR-9, PM-22, SI-18.
**Privacy Reporting.** Develop and submit privacy reports to oversight bodies and internal stakeholders.
blocks.practice: Through internal and external reporting, organizations promote accountability and transparency in organizational privacy operations. Reporting can also help organizations to determine progress in meeting privacy compliance requirements and privacy controls, compare performance across the federal government, discover vulnerabilities, identify gaps in policy and implementation, and identify models for success.
blocks.example: An annual privacy report goes to the board and the data protection regulator where required.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop [Assignment: organization-defined privacy reports] and disseminate to:
**a.1.** [Assignment: organization-defined oversight bodies] to demonstrate accountability with statutory, regulatory, and policy privacy mandates; and
**a.2.** [Assignment: organization-defined officials] and other personnel with responsibility for monitoring privacy program compliance; and
**b.** Review and update privacy reports [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** IR-9, PM-19.
**Risk Framing.** Identify and document risk framing: assumptions, constraints, priorities, trade-offs and risk tolerance.
blocks.practice: Risk framing is most effective when conducted at the organization level and in consultation with stakeholders throughout the organization including mission, business, and system owners.
blocks.example: Risk framing documents state that customer data confidentiality takes priority over availability of marketing systems.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Identify and document:
**a.1.** Assumptions affecting risk assessments, risk responses, and risk monitoring;
**a.2.** Constraints affecting risk assessments, risk responses, and risk monitoring;
**a.3.** Priorities and trade-offs considered by the organization for managing risk; and
**a.4.** Organizational risk tolerance;
**b.** Distribute the results of risk framing activities to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel] ; and
**c.** Review and update risk framing considerations [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** CA-7, PM-9, RA-3, RA-7.

sections.title: PM-29 Risk Management Program Leadership Roles

blocks.text: **Risk Management Program Leadership Roles.** Appoint a senior accountable official for risk management and establish a risk executive function.
blocks.practice: The senior accountable official for risk management leads the risk executive (function) in organization-wide risk management activities.
blocks.example: A risk executive committee chaired by the CRO oversees organisation-wide risk decisions.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Appoint a Senior Accountable Official for Risk Management to align organizational information security and privacy management processes with strategic, operational, and budgetary planning processes; and
**b.** Establish a Risk Executive (function) to view and analyze risk from an organization-wide perspective and ensure management of risk is consistent across the organization.

blocks.text: **Related controls:** PM-2, PM-19.

sections.title: PM-30 Supply Chain Risk Management Strategy

blocks.text: **Supply Chain Risk Management Strategy.** Develop an organisation-wide supply chain risk management strategy.
blocks.practice: An organization-wide supply chain risk management strategy includes an unambiguous expression of the supply chain risk appetite and tolerance for the organization, acceptable supply chain risk mitigation strategies or controls, a process for consistently evaluating and monitoring supply chain risk, approaches for implementing and communicating the supply chain risk management strategy, and the associated roles and responsibilities.
blocks.example: The C-SCRM strategy defines supplier tiering, assessment requirements and critical supplier monitoring.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop an organization-wide strategy for managing supply chain risks associated with the development, acquisition, maintenance, and disposal of systems, system components, and system services;
**b.** Implement the supply chain risk management strategy consistently across the organization; and
**c.** Review and update the supply chain risk management strategy on [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] or as required, to address organizational changes.

blocks.text: Enhancements (1 active)

rows: **PM-30(1)** Suppliers of Critical or Mission-essential Items

blocks.text: **Related controls:** CM-10, PM-9, SR-1, SR-2, SR-3, SR-4, SR-5, SR-6, SR-7, SR-8, SR-9, SR-11.
**Continuous Monitoring Strategy.** Develop an organisation-wide continuous monitoring strategy and implement programmes consistent with it.
blocks.practice: Continuous monitoring at the organization level facilitates ongoing awareness of the security and privacy posture across the organization to support organizational risk management decisions. The terms "continuous" and "ongoing" imply that organizations assess and monitor their controls and risks at a frequency sufficient to support risk-based decisions.
blocks.example: The strategy defines which metrics are monitored enterprise-wide, how often, and who receives them.

blocks.text: Control statement
Develop an organization-wide continuous monitoring strategy and implement continuous monitoring programs that include:

items: **a.** Establishing the following organization-wide metrics to be monitored: [Assignment: organization-defined metrics];
**b.** Establishing [Assignment: organization-defined monitoring frequencies] and [Assignment: organization-defined assessment frequencies] for control effectiveness;
**c.** Ongoing monitoring of organizationally-defined metrics in accordance with the continuous monitoring strategy;
**d.** Correlation and analysis of information generated by control assessments and monitoring;
**e.** Response actions to address results of the analysis of control assessment and monitoring information; and

**f.** Reporting the security and privacy status of organizational systems to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined personnel or roles] [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined frequency].

blocks.text: **Related controls:** AC-2, AC-6, AC-17, AT-4, AU-6, AU-13, CA-2, CA-5, CA-6, CA-7, CM-3, CM-4, CM-6, CM-11, IA-5, IR-5 and 34 more.
**Purposing.** Analyse systems and components supporting mission-essential services to ensure they're used only for their intended purpose.
blocks.practice: Systems are designed to support a specific mission or business function. However, over time, systems and system components may be used to support services and functions that are outside of the scope of the intended mission or business functions. This can result in exposing information resources to unintended environments and uses that can significantly increase threat exposure.
blocks.example: Review of a legacy server reveals it now also hosts an unrelated tool, which is moved elsewhere.

blocks.text: Control statement

Analyze [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components] supporting mission essential services or functions to ensure that the information resources are being used consistent with their intended purpose.
**Related controls:** CA-7, PL-2, RA-3, RA-9.
