**b.** Implement specific procedures for [Assignment: organization-defined authorized individuals] to manually disable hardware write-protect for firmware modifications and re-enable the write-protect prior to returning to operational mode.

blocks.text: **Policy and Procedures.** Maintain a system and information integrity policy and procedures, owned and reviewed on schedule.
blocks.practice: System and information integrity policy and procedures address the controls in the SI family that are implemented within systems and organizations. The risk management strategy is an important factor in establishing such policies and procedures. Policies and procedures contribute to security and privacy assurance.
blocks.example: IT security owns the integrity policy covering patching, malware protection and monitoring.

items: **a.** Develop, document, and disseminate to [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined personnel or roles]:

sections.title: SI-5 Security Alerts, Advisories, and Directives

blocks.text: **Security Alerts, Advisories, and Directives.** Receive security alerts, advisories and directives from external sources, disseminate them and implement them.
blocks.practice: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) generates security alerts and advisories to maintain situational awareness throughout the Federal Government. Security directives are issued by OMB or other designated organizations with the responsibility and authority to issue such directives.

blocks.text: **Security and Privacy Function Verification.** Verify correct operation of security and privacy functions and alert on failures.
blocks.practice: Transitional states for systems include system startup, restart, shutdown, and abort. System notifications include hardware indicator lights, electronic alerts to system administrators, and messages to local computer consoles.
blocks.example: Automated checks confirm the logging agent and EDR are running and alert if disabled.

sections.title: SI-7 Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity

blocks.text: **Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity.** Detect unauthorised changes to software, firmware and information using integrity verification tools.
blocks.practice: Unauthorized changes to software, firmware, and information can occur due to errors or malicious activity. Software includes operating systems (with key internal components, such as kernels or drivers), middleware, and applications. Firmware interfaces include Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) and Basic Input/Output System (BIOS).
blocks.example: File integrity monitoring alerts on changes to web server binaries and configuration files.

**Spam Protection.** Employ spam protection at entry and exit points and update it.
blocks.practice: System entry and exit points include firewalls, remote-access servers, electronic mail servers, web servers, proxy servers, workstations, notebook computers, and mobile devices. Spam can be transported by different means, including email, email attachments, and web accesses. Spam protection mechanisms include signature definitions.
blocks.example: The email gateway filters spam and phishing, with rules updated automatically.

**Information Input Validation.** Check the validity of information inputs.
blocks.practice: Checking the valid syntax and semantics of system inputs—including character set, length, numerical range, and acceptable values—verifies that inputs match specified definitions for format and content.

blocks.text: **Error Handling.** Generate error messages that give needed information without revealing information that could be exploited, and reveal details only to authorised staff.
blocks.practice: Organizations consider the structure and content of error messages. The extent to which systems can handle error conditions is guided and informed by organizational policy and operational requirements.
blocks.example: Users see a generic error page while detailed stack traces go only to protected logs.

items: **a.** Generate error messages that provide information necessary for corrective actions without revealing information that could be exploited; and
**b.** Reveal error messages only to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles].

**Information Management and Retention.** Manage and retain information within the system and its outputs according to laws, policies and requirements.
blocks.practice: Information management and retention requirements cover the full life cycle of information, in some cases extending beyond system disposal. Information to be retained may also include policies, procedures, plans, reports, data output from control implementation, and other types of administrative information.
blocks.example: Records retention schedules are applied automatically to email and document stores.

**Predictable Failure Prevention.** Determine the mean time to failure of components and provide substitute components and failover.
blocks.practice: While MTTF is primarily a reliability issue, predictable failure prevention is intended to address potential failures of system components that provide security capabilities. Failure rates reflect installation-specific consideration rather than the industry-average.
blocks.example: Disks nearing expected failure are replaced proactively, with hot spares in place.

**Non-persistence.** Implement non-persistent components that start in a known state and are refreshed periodically.
blocks.practice: Implementation of non-persistent components and services mitigates risk from advanced persistent threats (APTs) by reducing the targeting capability of adversaries (i.e., window of opportunity and available attack surface) to initiate and complete attacks.
blocks.example: Virtual desktops are rebuilt from a clean image at every logoff.

**Information Output Filtering.** Validate information output from software programs to ensure it is consistent with expected content.
blocks.practice: Certain types of attacks, including SQL injections, produce output results that are unexpected or inconsistent with the output results that would be expected from software programs or applications. Information output filtering focuses on detecting extraneous content, preventing such extraneous content from being displayed, and then alerting monitoring tools that anomalous behavior has been discovered.
blocks.example: A reporting system blocks outputs containing unmasked card numbers.

**Memory Protection.** Implement controls to protect system memory from unauthorised code execution.
blocks.practice: Some adversaries launch attacks with the intent of executing code in non-executable regions of memory or in memory locations that are prohibited. Controls employed to protect memory include data execution prevention and address space layout randomization. Data execution prevention controls can either be hardware-enforced or software-enforced with hardware enforcement providing the greater strength of mechanism.
blocks.example: Data execution prevention and address space layout randomisation are enabled on all servers.

blocks.text: Control statement

**Fail-safe Procedures.** Implement defined fail-safe procedures when defined failures occur.
blocks.practice: Failure conditions include the loss of communications among critical system components or between system components and operational facilities. Fail-safe procedures include alerting operator personnel and providing specific instructions on subsequent steps to take.
blocks.example: If the medication dispensing system loses connectivity, it reverts to a manual verification procedure.

sections.title: SI-18 Personally Identifiable Information Quality Operations

blocks.text: **Personally Identifiable Information Quality Operations.** Check the accuracy, relevance, timeliness and completeness of PII throughout its life cycle and correct inaccuracies.
blocks.practice: Personally identifiable information quality operations include the steps that organizations take to confirm the accuracy and relevance of personally identifiable information throughout the information life cycle. The information life cycle includes the creation, collection, use, processing, storage, maintenance, dissemination, disclosure, and disposal of personally identifiable information.
blocks.example: Customer address data is validated against postal records and customers can update it online.

items: **a.** Check the accuracy, relevance, timeliness, and completeness of personally identifiable information across the information life cycle [Assignment: organization-defined organization-defined frequency] ; and

**De-identification.** Remove identifiers from datasets (de-identification) and evaluate effectiveness against re-identification.
blocks.practice: De-identification is the general term for the process of removing the association between a set of identifying data and the data subject. Many datasets contain information about individuals that can be used to distinguish or trace an individual’s identity, such as name, social security number, date and place of birth, mother’s maiden name, or biometric records.
blocks.example: Research datasets are de-identified and tested for re-identification risk before sharing.

**Tainting.** Embed data or capabilities (taints) in systems or data to detect exfiltration or improper removal.
blocks.practice: Many cyber-attacks target organizational information, or information that the organization holds on behalf of other entities (e.g., personally identifiable information), and exfiltrate that data. In addition, insider attacks and erroneous user procedures can remove information from the system that is in violation of the organizational policies. Tainting approaches can range from passive to active.
blocks.example: Canary records in a customer database alert if they appear outside the organisation.

blocks.text: Control statement

**Related controls:** AU-13.
**Information Refresh.** Refresh information at defined frequencies or generate it on demand and delete it when no longer needed.
blocks.practice: Retaining information for longer than it is needed makes it an increasingly valuable and enticing target for adversaries. Keeping information available for the minimum period of time needed to support organizational missions or business functions reduces the opportunity for adversaries to compromise, capture, and exfiltrate that information.
blocks.example: Temporary access tokens are regenerated frequently and deleted after use.

blocks.text: Control statement

**Related controls:** SI-14.
**Information Diversity.** Identify alternative sources of information for essential functions and use them if primary sources are corrupted.
blocks.practice: Actions taken by a system service or a function are often driven by the information it receives. Corruption, fabrication, modification, or deletion of that information could impact the ability of the service function to properly carry out its intended actions. By having multiple sources of input, the service or function can continue operation if one source is corrupted or no longer available.
blocks.example: Two independent market data feeds allow traders to detect and switch away from a corrupted feed.

blocks.text: **Information Fragmentation.** Fragment information across multiple locations based on circumstances.
blocks.practice: One objective of the advanced persistent threat is to exfiltrate valuable information. Once exfiltrated, there is generally no way for the organization to recover the lost information. Therefore, organizations may consider dividing the information into disparate elements and distributing those elements across multiple systems or system components and locations.
blocks.example: Sensitive keys are split into shares stored in different locations.

sections.title: SR-2 Supply Chain Risk Management Plan

blocks.text: **Supply Chain Risk Management Plan.** Develop a plan for managing supply chain risks for the system and review and update it.
blocks.practice: The dependence on products, systems, and services from external providers, as well as the nature of the relationships with those providers, present an increasing level of risk to an organization.
blocks.example: The C-SCRM plan for the payment platform identifies critical suppliers and required assurances.

sections.title: SR-3 Supply Chain Controls and Processes

blocks.text: **Supply Chain Controls and Processes.** Establish a process to identify and address weaknesses in supply chain elements and processes, and employ supply chain controls.
blocks.practice: Supply chain elements include organizations, entities, or tools employed for the research and development, design, manufacturing, acquisition, delivery, integration, operations and maintenance, and disposal of systems and system components.

**Provenance.** Document, monitor and maintain valid provenance of systems, components and data.
blocks.practice: Every system and system component has a point of origin and may be changed throughout its existence. Provenance is the chronology of the origin, development, ownership, location, and changes to a system or system component and associated data. It may also include personnel and processes used to interact with or make modifications to the system, component, or associated data.
blocks.example: The origin and chain of custody of network hardware is tracked from manufacturer to installation.

sections.title: SR-5 Acquisition Strategies, Tools, and Methods

blocks.text: **Acquisition Strategies, Tools, and Methods.** Use acquisition strategies, contract tools and procurement methods to protect against supply chain risks.
blocks.practice: The use of the acquisition process provides an important vehicle to protect the supply chain. There are many useful tools and techniques available, including obscuring the end use of a system or system component, using blind or filtered buys, requiring tamper-evident packaging, or using trusted or controlled distribution.
blocks.example: Critical hardware is bought only from authorised distributors with anti-counterfeit clauses.

blocks.practice: An assessment and review of supplier risk includes security and supply chain risk management processes, foreign ownership, control or influence (FOCI), and the ability of the supplier to effectively assess subordinate second-tier and third-tier suppliers and contractors. The reviews may be conducted by the organization or by an independent third party.

**Tamper Resistance and Detection.** Implement a tamper protection programme for systems and components.
blocks.practice: Anti-tamper technologies, tools, and techniques provide a level of protection for systems, system components, and services against many threats, including reverse engineering, modification, and substitution. Strong identification combined with tamper resistance and/or tamper detection is essential to protecting systems and components during distribution and when in use.
blocks.example: Tamper-evident seals are applied to network devices shipped to remote sites.

blocks.text: Control statement
Implement a tamper protection program for the system, system component, or system service.

sections.title: SR-10 Inspection of Systems or Components

blocks.text: **Inspection of Systems or Components.** Inspect systems or components for evidence of tampering at defined times or triggers.
blocks.practice: The inspection of systems or systems components for tamper resistance and detection addresses physical and logical tampering and is applied to systems and system components removed from organization-controlled areas.
blocks.example: Laptops returning from high-risk travel are inspected for signs of tampering.

blocks.text: Control statement

Inspect the following systems or system components [Selection (one or more): at random; at [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] ; upon [Assignment: organization-defined indications of need for inspection] ] to detect tampering: [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components].
**Related controls:** AT-3, PM-30, SI-4, SI-7, SR-3, SR-4, SR-5, SR-9, SR-11.
**Component Authenticity.** Develop and implement anti-counterfeit policy and procedures to detect and prevent counterfeit components, and report them.
blocks.practice: Sources of counterfeit components include manufacturers, developers, vendors, and contractors. Anti-counterfeiting policies and procedures support tamper resistance and provide a level of protection against the introduction of malicious code. External reporting organizations include CISA.
blocks.example: Components are verified against manufacturer serial databases; suspected counterfeits are reported.

blocks.text: Control statement

items: **a.** Develop and implement anti-counterfeit policy and procedures that include the means to detect and prevent counterfeit components from entering the system; and

**b.** Report counterfeit system components to [Selection (one or more): source of counterfeit component; [Assignment: organization-defined external reporting organizations] ; [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] ].

**Component Disposal.** Dispose of data, documentation, tools or system components using defined techniques and methods.
blocks.practice: Data, documentation, tools, or system components can be disposed of at any time during the system development life cycle (not only in the disposal or retirement phase of the life cycle). For example, disposal can occur during research and development, design, prototyping, or operations/maintenance and include methods such as disk cleaning, removal of cryptographic keys, partial reuse of components.
blocks.example: Retired network devices have configurations wiped and are destroyed by a certified vendor.

Account Management. Manage the full lifecycle of system accounts: define account types, approve creation, assign managers, monitor use, and disable or remove accounts when no longer needed. Baselines: L M H
Access Enforcement. Enforce approved authorisations so that users and processes can only access what they have been permitted to access. Baselines: L M H
Least Privilege. Give users and processes only the privileges they need to perform assigned tasks. Baselines: M H
Remote Access. Establish and authorise usage restrictions and configuration for each type of remote access before allowing it. Baselines: L M H

Literacy Training and Awareness. Provide security and privacy literacy training to all users at onboarding and periodically, including insider-threat and social engineering awareness. Baselines: L M H P
Event Logging. Identify the types of events the system must log, coordinated with other functions, and review the list periodically. Baselines: L M H P
Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting. Review and analyse audit records for signs of inappropriate or unusual activity and report findings. Baselines: L M H
Control Assessments. Plan and conduct control assessments with an appropriate team, and report results to stakeholders. Baselines: L M H P
Plan of Action and Milestones. Develop and update a plan of action and milestones (POA&M) for weaknesses found in assessments and monitoring. Baselines: L M H P
Authorization. Assign a senior official to authorise the system to operate (and common controls), accepting the residual risk, and update authorisations periodically. Baselines: L M H P
Continuous Monitoring. Develop and run a continuous monitoring strategy with defined metrics, frequencies, analysis and reporting. Baselines: L M H P
Baseline Configuration. Develop, document and maintain a current baseline configuration of the system under configuration control. Baselines: L M H
Configuration Settings. Establish and document mandatory configuration settings using secure baselines, implement them and monitor deviations. Baselines: L M H
Least Functionality. Configure the system to provide only essential capabilities, prohibiting or restricting unneeded functions, ports, protocols and services. Baselines: L M H
System Component Inventory. Develop and maintain an accurate, complete inventory of system components at the level needed for tracking and reporting. Baselines: L M H
Contingency Plan. Develop, approve, distribute and maintain a contingency plan covering essential functions, recovery objectives, roles, and restoration. Baselines: L M H
System Backup. Back up user data, system data and documentation at defined frequencies, protect the backups and test them. Baselines: L M H

Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users). Uniquely identify and authenticate organisational users and processes acting for them. Enhancements add MFA and replay resistance. Baselines: L M H
Authenticator Management. Manage authenticators (passwords, tokens, certificates, keys): initial distribution, strength, protection, changes and revocation. Baselines: L M H
Incident Handling. Implement incident handling covering preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication and recovery, coordinated with contingency planning. Baselines: L M H P
Incident Response Plan. Develop, approve and maintain an incident response plan that provides a roadmap for the capability. Baselines: L M H P
Media Sanitization. Sanitise media before disposal, release out of organisational control or reuse, using methods appropriate to the information. Baselines: L M H P
System Security and Privacy Plans. Develop and maintain system security and privacy plans that describe the system, its boundary, environment, and how controls are implemented. Baselines: L M H P
Security Categorization. Categorise the system and its information based on potential impact (e.g. FIPS 199) and have the categorisation approved. Baselines: L M H
Risk Assessment. Conduct risk assessments of threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact, integrate results, document them and update periodically. Baselines: L M H P
Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning. Monitor and scan for vulnerabilities, analyse reports, remediate within defined times and share information. Baselines: L M H
Security and Privacy Engineering Principles. Apply systems security and privacy engineering principles in specifying, designing, developing and modifying systems. Baselines: L M H
Unsupported System Components. Replace system components when they are no longer supported, or provide justification and alternative support. Baselines: L M H
Boundary Protection. Monitor and control communications at external and key internal boundaries, using managed interfaces and separating publicly accessible components. Baselines: L M H
Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity. Protect the confidentiality and integrity of transmitted information. Baselines: M H
Cryptographic Protection. Determine required cryptographic uses and implement the types of cryptography required for each. Baselines: L M H
Protection of Information at Rest. Protect the confidentiality and integrity of information at rest. Baselines: M H
Flaw Remediation. Identify, report and correct system flaws; test updates; install security updates within defined times; incorporate flaw remediation into configuration management. Baselines: L M H
Malicious Code Protection. Implement malicious code protection at entry and exit points, update it, scan periodically and respond to detections. Baselines: L M H
System Monitoring. Monitor the system to detect attacks, indicators of attack and unauthorised use, using internal and external monitoring. Baselines: L M H
Supply Chain Controls and Processes. Establish a process to identify and address weaknesses in supply chain elements and processes, and employ supply chain controls. Baselines: L M H
